name: Classic-Style Test 4
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: At the Brannock reservoir, swallows nesting under the high eaves of the old pump house fledge far more chicks per nest than do swallows nesting under the low footbridge nearby. Rats from the reservoir bank can easily climb to nests under the footbridge but cannot reach those under the pump-house eaves. Predation by rats, therefore, probably accounts for the difference.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Swallows at the pump house tend to lay their eggs earlier in the season than do swallows at the footbridge.
Rats are known to eat the eggs and nestlings of many kinds of birds, including several species of swallow.
Far more people walk past the footbridge nests each day than walk past the nests under the pump-house eaves.
Footbridge nests with rat guards last year fledged about as many chicks per nest as pump-house nests did.
Rats from the reservoir bank have often been seen near the footbridge during the weeks when the swallows are nesting.
questions.explanation: If footbridge nests protected from rats do as well as pump-house nests, the location itself isn’t the problem and rats are, which strongly supports the causal claim; that is (D). (E) is tempting but only confirms what the argument already grants, that rats can get to the footbridge nests. (B) shows rats eat swallow nestlings in general, not that they explain this difference. (A) and (C) offer alternative causes and so weaken the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Rat predation probably explains why footbridge nests fledge fewer chicks than pump-house nests.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Footbridge nests fledge fewer chicks; rats can reach footbridge nests but not pump-house nests.

breakdown.analysis: Rats can reach the footbridge nests, sure. But lots of things differ between a low footbridge and high eaves: people, noise, timing, shade. How do we know it’s the rats? The best support is a test: take away the rats and see if the difference disappears. We need an answer that isolates rats as the cause or rules out the other differences.

choices.note: This hands you an alternative cause: earlier breeders might simply do better. That weakens the argument.
Tempting, because it shows rats can do the damage, even to swallows. But that’s general. It doesn’t show rats are what explains this particular gap between two sites.
Another alternative cause: human disturbance could be what hurts the footbridge nests. That weakens.
CORRECT. Same footbridge, rats blocked, and the nests do as well as the pump-house nests. That pins the difference on rats rather than on the location itself.

Tempting, because it puts rats right next to the footbridge nests. But the argument already grants that rats can reach those nests. Showing that rats are around corroborates a premise; it does nothing to show that rats, rather than something else about the footbridge, explain the gap.

questions.stimulus:
Moreno: The warehouse workers’ union should accept the company’s contract offer. It raises wages 4 percent a year for three years, which is more than workers at any other warehouse in the region received in their most recent contracts.

Lyle: That raise is certainly generous. But the offer also lets the company require overtime on only one day’s notice, and workers with young children cannot arrange child care that quickly. The union should reject the offer unless that clause is removed.
questions.stem: Moreno and Lyle disagree over whether
choices: the offered wage increase is larger than the increases that other warehouse workers in the region recently received
workers with young children would have difficulty arranging child care on one day’s notice
the union should accept the company’s offer in its current form
the company would agree to remove the overtime clause from its offer
the size of the wage increase is the most important feature of any contract offer
questions.explanation: Moreno says the union should accept the offer as made, while Lyle says it should be rejected unless the overtime clause comes out, so they disagree about accepting the offer in its current form, (C). (A) is tempting, but Lyle concedes the raise is generous and never disputes the regional comparison. Moreno says nothing about child care (B) or about which feature matters most (E), and neither speaker predicts what the company will do (D).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Moreno: accept the offer, because the raise beats every other warehouse in the region; Lyle: the raise is generous, but reject the offer unless the short-notice overtime clause is removed.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Lyle grants Moreno’s point about the raise, so that’s not the fight. The fight is the bottom line: Moreno says accept the offer as it stands; Lyle says don’t, not with that clause in it. We need an answer about accepting the current offer.

choices.note: Tempting, since it’s Moreno’s main reason. But Lyle calls the raise ‘certainly generous’ and never challenges the comparison. No disagreement here.
Lyle says yes, but Moreno says nothing about child care. One speaker silent means no disagreement you can prove.
CORRECT. Moreno: accept it. Lyle: reject it unless the clause is removed, so not in its current form. Clear yes versus no.
Neither speaker predicts what the company will do. Lyle only says what the union should do if the clause stays.
Too strong, and nobody says it. Moreno relies on the raise but never claims it’s the most important feature of every contract.

questions.stimulus: Fitness columnist: Many trainers doubt that ice baths do athletes any good. But last month our magazine’s website invited readers to report whether taking ice baths after hard workouts reduced their muscle soreness. Of the 900 readers who responded, 85 percent said that the ice baths had helped. So most athletes who take ice baths after hard workouts get real relief from soreness.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the fitness columnist’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: fails to consider that athletes may be able to reduce muscle soreness in ways other than taking ice baths
takes for granted that because ice baths help most athletes, they help every athlete who takes them
takes for granted that readers who chose to report their experiences are representative of athletes in general
presumes, without providing justification, that athletes who feel less sore after workouts also perform better
criticizes ice baths on the grounds that some of the readers who responded did not benefit from them
questions.explanation: The 900 respondents are magazine readers who chose to write in, and readers who got relief are the ones most motivated to report it, so they may not represent athletes generally; (C) names this unwarranted presumption about a self-selected sample. (A) is tempting because it sounds like a missed alternative, but the argument says nothing about ice baths being the only remedy, so other remedies don’t matter. (B) describes an overgeneralization the columnist never makes; the conclusion says ‘most,’ not ‘every.’

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most athletes who take ice baths after hard workouts get real relief from soreness.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 85 percent of the 900 website readers who chose to respond said ice baths helped.

breakdown.analysis: Who answers a ‘did ice baths help you?’ call on a fitness website? Mostly people who use ice baths and liked them. People who tried them, felt nothing, and moved on rarely bother to write in. That’s a self-selected sample, a classic sampling flaw; know it. It’s like a restaurant asking diners to post reviews and concluding most diners loved it because 85 percent of the reviews are glowing. We need an answer that says the sample picked itself and may not match athletes in general.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The columnist never says ice baths are the only way to reduce soreness. Other remedies existing doesn’t touch whether ice baths work for most athletes.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Stretching reduces soreness, so stretching is the only thing athletes need to recover from hard workouts.

choices.note: Too strong a description. The conclusion says ‘most athletes,’ not every athlete. The columnist doesn’t overgeneralize to each individual.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Ice baths relieve soreness for most athletes, so they will certainly relieve yours.

choices.note: CORRECT. The respondents volunteered, and people with good results are more likely to report them. The columnist simply takes for granted that this self-selected group matches athletes in general, and nothing supports that.
The argument never mentions performance. It’s only about feeling less sore. This answer adds a link the columnist didn’t make.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Athletes who take ice baths feel less sore, so ice baths must make them run faster.

choices.note: Opposite of what happens. The columnist praises ice baths; nothing in the argument criticizes them.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Fifteen percent of readers said ice baths didn’t help, so ice baths are worthless.

questions.stimulus: Many residents of Mossburn believe that the sinkholes that keep opening around town are caused by blasting at the quarry that opened four years ago. But sinkholes have opened in the Mossburn area at about the same rate for the past hundred years, both before and since the quarry opened, and they are just as common on the far side of the valley, well beyond the reach of the blasting. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the blasting at the quarry has made sinkholes in Mossburn more frequent than they would otherwise have been
the sinkholes in Mossburn and those on the far side of the valley are produced by the same underlying geological conditions
the blasting at the quarry has had no effect of any kind on the ground beneath Mossburn
the blasting at the quarry is probably not the cause of the sinkholes that keep opening in Mossburn
residents blame the quarry mainly because it opened at a time when sinkholes were drawing more public attention
questions.explanation: The argument sets up the residents’ belief and then gives two reasons to doubt it: the sinkhole rate hasn’t changed since the quarry opened, and sinkholes are just as common where the blasting can’t reach. The modest conclusion that the blasting probably isn’t the cause is (D). (C) is the tempting overstatement: the evidence counts against the blasting causing sinkholes, not against its having any effect on the ground at all. (B) names a specific common cause the argument never establishes.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Residents blame the quarry’s blasting for the sinkholes; 2. the sinkhole rate is the same before and since the quarry opened; 3. sinkholes are just as common far beyond the blasting’s reach. The blank is the author’s conclusion.

breakdown.analysis: The word “But” tells you the author is pushing back on the residents. If blasting caused the sinkholes, you’d expect more of them after the quarry opened and fewer where the blasting can’t reach. Neither is true. So the blank should say, modestly, that the blasting probably isn’t the culprit. Watch for answers that push further than the evidence: “no effect of any kind,” or a specific cause the author never names.

choices.note: The opposite of the author’s point. A steady rate before and after the quarry opened is evidence that the blasting has not increased the sinkholes.

Tempting, because sinkholes on both sides of the valley suggest something they share. But the author never says what causes them, and “the same underlying geological conditions” is a specific causal claim the facts don’t establish. The author only needs to show the quarry is probably not to blame.

Too strong. The evidence is about sinkholes. The blasting could rattle windows or crack foundations without causing a single sinkhole, so “no effect of any kind” goes beyond anything the author shows.

CORRECT. The rate didn’t change when the quarry opened, and sinkholes are just as common out of the blasting’s reach. That is exactly the evidence for “probably not the cause,” hedged the way the facts allow.
We don’t know why residents blame the quarry. The author rebuts the belief; the author never explains where it came from.

questions.stimulus: Since the thermostat on Tavola Pizzeria’s only oven began malfunctioning, causing the oven to run considerably hotter than its setting, the restaurant has had to throw out many overcooked trays of roasted vegetables. Yet over the same period, customers have rated Tavola’s pizza crusts much more highly than before, even though the pizzas are baked in the same oven.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Customers who order pizza at Tavola seldom also order the roasted vegetables served there.
Tavola’s pizza recipe calls for an oven temperature well below the one at which crust crisps and browns best.
Since the malfunction began, Tavola’s cooks have been checking pizzas more often while they bake.
Tavola’s vegetables are roasted on the oven’s upper rack, where the excess heat from the faulty thermostat is greatest.
Many pizzerias use one oven for their pizzas and a separate oven for roasted dishes.
questions.explanation: If the recipe’s set temperature was too low for an ideal crust, an oven running hotter than its setting would push pizzas closer to the best temperature while overshooting for vegetables, so the defect helps the crust; that is (B). (C) is tempting, but checking more often could at most keep pizzas from burning; it doesn’t explain why crusts got better than before. (D) explains only the ruined vegetables. (A) and (E) don’t address why the same overheating improved the pizza.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The oven runs too hot and ruins vegetables, but pizzas from the same oven are now rated better than before.

breakdown.analysis: How can a broken oven make anything better? Only if the old temperature was wrong for pizza in the first place. Then ‘too hot’ for vegetables could be ‘just right’ for crust. It’s like a car whose speedometer reads low: a driver who always went too slow suddenly arrives on time. We need an answer showing the extra heat moves pizza toward its ideal, not away from it.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Who orders what doesn’t change what the oven does to the pizza.
CORRECT. If the recipe’s temperature was below the best crust temperature, the extra heat fixes the crust while still overcooking the vegetables. The defect turns out to help.

Tempting, because it shows the cooks reacting to the problem. But extra checking could only prevent burned pizzas. It doesn’t explain why crusts are rated better than they were before the malfunction.
Tempting, because it explains why the vegetables suffer so badly. But it explains only one side. It says nothing about why the pizza crusts are rated better than they were before the malfunction.
Right topic, wrong group. Tavola uses one oven for both; what other pizzerias do is irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Urban planner: Several cities near Halvern have converted their downtown one-way streets back to two-way traffic, and merchants there report busier sidewalks. Halvern’s Pike and Orrin Streets were laid out decades ago as a one-way pair to speed commuters through downtown. Most commuters now take the new bypass, however, so that design no longer serves its purpose. Halvern would do well to follow its neighbors’ example, since two-way streets also slow cars enough to make sidewalks more inviting to shoppers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the urban planner’s argument?
choices: Merchants in nearby cities that have converted one-way streets to two-way traffic report busier sidewalks than before.
Halvern should make Pike and Orrin Streets two-way, as several nearby cities have done with comparable streets.
The one-way layout of Pike and Orrin Streets no longer serves the purpose for which it was originally adopted.
Two-way streets slow cars enough to make the sidewalks along them more inviting to shoppers.
Most of the commuters who once drove through downtown Halvern now travel on the new bypass instead.
questions.explanation: Everything in the argument supports the recommendation in the last sentence, that Halvern should follow its neighbors and make Pike and Orrin two-way; (B) restates it. (C) is the trap: it is flagged by “so,” but it is an intermediate conclusion that in turn supports the recommendation. (A), (D), and (E) are premises.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Halvern should follow its neighbors and convert Pike and Orrin Streets to two-way traffic.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nearby cities converted and their sidewalks got busier; most commuters now use the bypass, so the one-way design no longer serves its purpose; two-way streets make sidewalks more inviting.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The nearby cities are a precedent; the bypass point leads to “so that design no longer serves its purpose”; and the “since” clause gives one more reason. All of it points at “Halvern would do well to follow its neighbors’ example,” which means: convert Pike and Orrin to two-way. Don’t be fooled by “so” in the middle. It flags a subsidiary conclusion that is itself a reason for the recommendation.

choices.note: A premise. The neighbors’ experience is offered as a reason for Halvern to follow them.
CORRECT. “Follow its neighbors’ example” means doing what they did: making the one-way pair two-way. Every other statement is offered in support of this.

Tempting, because “so” flags it as a conclusion. But it is an intermediate step: the design’s being obsolete is a reason to convert the streets. It supports the recommendation; it isn’t the recommendation.
A premise, introduced by “since.” It is one more reason to convert the streets.
A premise. The bypass fact supports the intermediate conclusion that the one-way design has outlived its purpose.

questions.stimulus: Many older customers of Linden Street Pharmacy have trouble opening child-resistant medicine bottles, and some of them stop taking their medications as a result. Any customer can ask for easy-open caps instead, but few customers know this. So if the pharmacy posts signs at its counter announcing that easy-open caps are available on request, fewer of its older customers will stop taking their medications.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Most older customers who stop taking their medications do so mainly because they are unable to open the child-resistant bottles.
Easy-open caps cost the pharmacy no more than child-resistant caps do.
Older customers are more likely than younger customers to stop taking the medications that have been prescribed to them.
Some older customers who have trouble opening child-resistant bottles would notice the signs and ask for easy-open caps.
Signs at the counter are the most effective way to let customers know that easy-open caps are available on request.
questions.explanation: The plan works only if the signs actually reach some of the customers who struggle with the caps and lead them to ask for easy-open ones; negate (D) and the signs change nothing. (A) is tempting, but the argument needs only some customers to be helped, not a majority of those who stop. (E) is too strong: the signs need to work, not to be the best method.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Posting signs about easy-open caps will lead fewer older customers to stop taking their medications.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Some older customers stop taking medications because they can’t open child-resistant bottles; easy-open caps are available on request; few customers know this.

breakdown.analysis: So what if there’s a sign? A sign only helps if someone who needs it sees it and acts on it. If every struggling customer ignored the sign or never asked, nothing would change. We need an answer that says at least some of the right customers will notice and ask. Assumption answers are often modest like this: ‘some,’ not ‘most.’

choices.note: Tempting, because it makes the caps sound like the main problem. But the argument only needs some customers to be helped. Negate it: even if most quit for other reasons, the ones who quit because of caps could still be helped. No damage.
choices.negation: Not most older customers who stop taking their medications do so mainly because they can’t open the bottles.

choices.note: Cost is a different dimension. Negate it: easy-open caps cost more. The signs could still keep customers on their medications. No damage.
choices.negation: Easy-open caps cost the pharmacy more than child-resistant caps do.

choices.note: An irrelevant comparison. Negate it: older customers are no more likely to stop than younger ones. The plan can still help the older ones who do stop. No damage.
choices.negation: Older customers are not more likely than younger customers to stop taking their medications.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: none of the struggling customers would notice the signs and ask. Then the signs change nothing and the conclusion collapses.
choices.negation: No older customers who have trouble opening the bottles would notice the signs and ask for easy-open caps.

choices.note: Too strong. The signs only have to work, not be the best option. Negate it: some other method is more effective. The signs could still help. No damage.
choices.negation: Signs at the counter are not the most effective way to let customers know about easy-open caps.

questions.stimulus: Marketing director at Pellbrook Press: Every novel on this year’s Westmark Booksellers bestseller list, which ranks novels by their sales in independent bookstores, was promoted with a tour of podcast interviews, and several of those novels were written by first-time authors. So if we arrange podcast tours for our debut novelists this spring, their novels will make that list.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the marketing director’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: treats a feature shared by all the bestselling novels as enough to make a novel a bestseller
draws a conclusion about all novels from a sample that consists only of the novels of debut authors
fails to consider that the Westmark Booksellers list might not accurately reflect how well novels actually sell
takes for granted that Pellbrook’s debut novelists would be willing and able to go on podcast tours this spring
presumes, without providing justification, that podcast tours are the most effective form of book promotion
questions.explanation: Knowing that every bestseller had a podcast tour shows at most that such a tour goes along with making the list, not that a tour guarantees it; many toured novels may have missed the list. (A) names this necessary-versus-sufficient confusion. (E) is tempting, but the director never compares podcasts with other promotion. (D) is merely possible and wouldn’t fix the argument even if the novelists were eager.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If Pellbrook gives its debut novelists podcast tours, their novels will make the bestseller list.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every novel on this year’s bestseller list had a podcast tour.

breakdown.analysis: Bestseller → podcast tour. The director flips it into podcast tour → bestseller. That’s confusing a necessary condition with a sufficient one. The detail about first-time authors doesn’t help: it still only describes novels that made the list. Maybe hundreds of novels had podcast tours and sank without a trace. It’s like saying every Olympic sprinter wears running shoes, so if I buy running shoes I’ll make the Olympics. We need an answer that says the argument treats something all the winners share as a guarantee of winning.

choices.note: CORRECT. All the bestsellers had tours, so a tour may be necessary, but the director treats it as sufficient. Lots of toured novels could have missed the list.
Backwards. The evidence is about bestselling novels in general, and the conclusion is about debut novels, not the other way around.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The three debut novels we published did well, so every novel we publish will do well.

choices.note: Merely possible. Nothing suggests the list is unreliable, and the flaw remains even if the list is perfect.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our book topped the list, so it outsold everything else, even though the list counts only a few stores.

choices.note: Merely possible, and beside the point. Even if every novelist happily toured, a tour still wouldn’t guarantee a bestseller.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We’ll book our authors on a twenty-city tour, so they will certainly do all twenty events.

choices.note: Tempting, because the director clearly loves podcasts. But there’s no comparison with other promotion anywhere. The argument would be just as flawed if podcasts were the best method.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Podcast tours sold some books last year, so they’re clearly the best way to promote any novel.

questions.stimulus: Last season Ridgefield High School required every player on its soccer teams to wear a newly designed padded headband during all of its games and practices, at a cost of about forty dollars per player. Over the season, team trainers recorded 30 percent fewer head injuries among the school’s soccer players than they had recorded the season before. So the headbands made Ridgefield’s soccer players safer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Last season’s recorded head injuries, though fewer in number, included more concussions serious enough to sideline a player for weeks.
The headbands offer no protection against knee and ankle injuries, which are the most common injuries among soccer players.
At a rival school whose soccer players did not wear the headbands, recorded head injuries rose slightly over the same season.
In both seasons, the trainers recorded every head injury that occurred among the soccer players, no matter how minor.
Many of the players complained throughout the season that the headbands were hot, heavy, and uncomfortable to wear.
questions.explanation: The argument measures safety by the number of head injuries. If the remaining injuries were more often serious concussions, players may be no safer, or less safe, despite the lower count; that is (A). (B) is tempting because the conclusion says “safer,” but the headbands don’t cause knee injuries, so failing to prevent them doesn’t make players less safe than before. (C) and (D) if anything strengthen the argument, and (E) is about comfort, not safety.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The headbands made Ridgefield’s soccer players safer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Players wore the headbands all season; recorded head injuries fell 30 percent from the season before.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of injuries really the measure of safety? Ten scraped foreheads and one season-ending concussion aren’t the same thing. If the count went down but the injuries that remain are worse, “safer” doesn’t follow. We need an answer that shows the drop in the count hides a change in severity, or that offers another reason the count fell.

choices.note: CORRECT. Fewer injuries, but more serious concussions. The argument counted injuries and ignored how bad they were, so the 30 percent drop no longer shows the players are safer.
Tempting, because “safer” sounds broad. But the headbands don’t cause knee or ankle injuries; they just don’t prevent them. Players can still be safer than before overall. No damage.
This cuts the wrong way. Injuries rose at a school without headbands, which makes Ridgefield’s drop look more like a headband effect, not less.
This helps the argument if anything: the counts in both seasons are complete and comparable. It rules out a recording change as the explanation.
Comfort is a different dimension. Hot, heavy headbands can still prevent injuries.

questions.stimulus: Every worker at the Sayer foundry who took an unpaid leave of more than two weeks last year had that leave approved by the shop steward. The steward has never approved such a leave for a worker with fewer than three years of seniority, nor has she ever approved one that included any days in December. Ilse, who has worked at the foundry for five years, took an unpaid leave of three weeks last year.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: The steward approved Ilse’s leave in some month other than December.
Every worker with at least three years of seniority who requested a leave outside December last year had the leave approved.
Any worker who took an unpaid leave of two weeks or less last year did so without the steward’s approval.
Ilse’s leave was the longest unpaid leave taken by any foundry worker last year.
None of the days of the unpaid leave that Ilse took last year fell in the month of December.
questions.explanation: Ilse’s three-week leave last year was longer than two weeks, so the steward approved it, and the steward has never approved such a leave that included December days, so Ilse’s leave had none; that is (E). (A) is the trap: the rule limits which leaves were approved, not when the approval was given. (B) reverses a necessary condition into a sufficient one, and (C) and (D) go beyond the facts.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Unpaid leave over two weeks taken last year → approved by steward; 2. leave of that length approved by steward (ever) → at least three years’ seniority; 3. leave of that length approved by steward (ever) → no December days; 4. Ilse took a three-week unpaid leave last year.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: Ilse’s leave was over two weeks → approved by the steward → no December days (and Ilse has the seniority, which we already knew). Notice the steward’s rules say “never,” so it doesn’t matter when she signed off; any approval she gave obeys them. So we can prove Ilse’s leave had no December days. Watch for answers that reverse a link or quietly change what the rule is about.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the December rule. But the rule is about leaves that include December days, not about when the steward signed off. She could have approved Ilse’s June leave in December.
This reverses the seniority rule. Seniority is necessary for approval, not a guarantee of it.
We don’t know this. The facts only cover leaves longer than two weeks. Shorter leaves might also need approval; we’re told nothing about them.
Unsupported ranking. Nothing tells us how long anyone else’s leave was.
CORRECT. Over two weeks → approved → no December days. Ilse’s leave fits the chain, so none of it fell in December.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Parish registers from the farming villages of the Ostrand region show that, throughout the eighteenth century, weddings were concentrated in November and early December. Some scholars attribute this to a religious custom of marrying before Advent. The pattern more likely reflects the farming calendar, however: couples married once the grain harvest was in, when hired laborers had been paid their season’s wages and work was light.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historian’s argument?
choices: Ostrand’s fishing villages, whose churches followed the same religious customs as its farming villages, show no seasonal peak in weddings.
Throughout the eighteenth century, the church in Ostrand discouraged couples from marrying during Advent and during Lent.
In years when Ostrand’s grain harvest came in unusually late, the peak in weddings recorded in the registers did not shift later.
Some of the couples who married in Ostrand’s farming villages came from landowning families rather than from families of hired laborers.
Customs concerning the proper season for weddings varied considerably from one region of the country to another.
questions.explanation: Two explanations compete for the November wedding peak: religious custom and the farming calendar. Villages that share the religious custom but don’t farm are a test case. If they show no peak, the custom alone doesn’t produce one, which favors the farming explanation; that is (A). (B) is tempting because it mentions Advent, but it supports the scholars’ religious explanation. (C) weakens the historian: if the peak doesn’t move with the harvest, the harvest probably isn’t driving it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The November–December wedding peak in Ostrand’s farming villages reflects the farming calendar, not a religious custom of marrying before Advent.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Weddings cluster right after the grain harvest, when laborers had been paid and work was light.

breakdown.analysis: Two hypotheses explain the same pattern equally well, so the historian’s evidence doesn’t pick between them. How would you test them? Find a group that has one cause but not the other. Villages with the same church customs but no grain harvest: if religion drives the peak, they should show it too; if farming does, they shouldn’t. We need an answer that separates the two causes, or that ties the peak more tightly to the harvest.

choices.note: CORRECT. Same religious customs, no farming, and no peak. The custom by itself doesn’t create the November cluster, so the farming calendar is the better explanation. It’s a control group in disguise.

Tempting, because it’s the only answer that mentions Advent. But a church discouraging weddings during Advent is a reason to marry just before it, which is the scholars’ explanation, not the historian’s.
This cuts the wrong way. If the harvest came late and the wedding peak stayed put, the peak isn’t tracking the harvest. That weakens the historian.
So? Both explanations apply to landowners and laborers alike. Knowing that some couples weren’t laborers doesn’t favor the farming calendar over religious custom.
Vague and beside the point. Variation elsewhere in the country says nothing about which explanation fits Ostrand.

questions.stimulus: Curator: Dr. Brandt proposes that the Hollis Museum accept every piece of furniture made before 1900 that is offered to it, on the grounds that age alone gives an object historic value. But under that standard, a mass-produced 1895 pine kitchen stool would merit the same place in the collection as the carved desk at which the state constitution was signed. No one seriously regards such a stool as a historic treasure. So age alone cannot be what gives an object historic value.
questions.stem: The claim that the kitchen stool would merit the same place in the collection as the carved desk plays which one of the following roles in the curator’s argument?
choices: It is an implication of Dr. Brandt’s standard that, together with another claim, is used to undermine the standard’s rationale.
It is offered in support of the claim that no one seriously regards a mass-produced pine kitchen stool as a historic treasure.
It is a premise that Dr. Brandt offers in support of the proposal to accept every piece of furniture made before 1900.
It is a claim the curator accepts and uses to argue that the carved desk deserves a less prominent place in the collection.
It is the main conclusion of the argument, which the claim that no one regards the stool as a historic treasure is offered to support.
questions.explanation: The curator derives the stool claim from Brandt’s age-only standard and pairs it with the claim that no one regards such a stool as a historic treasure; together they discredit the idea that age alone confers historic value. (A) describes this. (B) is the near-miss: the two claims sit side by side, but the stool claim doesn’t support the “no one regards it as a treasure” claim; they work together against the standard. (E) mistakes a premise for the conclusion, which is the last sentence.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Age alone cannot be what gives an object historic value.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brandt’s age-only standard would give a mass-produced 1895 kitchen stool the same place as the desk where the state constitution was signed; no one thinks such a stool is a historic treasure.

breakdown.analysis: This is a “reduce it to absurdity” move. The curator says: follow Brandt’s rule and you get a ridiculous result, a factory-made kitchen stool earns the same place as the constitution desk. The author doesn’t believe the stool deserves that. The claim is what the rule implies, and the next sentence (no one sees such a stool as a treasure) is what makes the implication unacceptable. Together they sink the rule’s rationale, that age alone gives historic value. We need an answer that calls the claim a consequence of Brandt’s standard used against it. Watch the relation as well as the role: which claim supports which?

choices.note: CORRECT. “An implication of Dr. Brandt’s standard” is the stool claim; “another claim” is that no one regards such a stool as a historic treasure; “the standard’s rationale” is that age alone gives historic value, which the conclusion rejects.

Tempting, because the two claims sit side by side. But the stool claim doesn’t give any reason to think nobody regards the stool as a treasure. That claim stands on its own; the two are combined to attack the standard. Right neighborhood, wrong relation.
Brandt never mentions the stool. The curator brings it up, against Brandt.
The curator doesn’t accept that the stool deserves the desk’s place, and nothing knocks the desk. It’s the obvious treasure the stool is compared with.
The main conclusion is the last sentence: age alone can’t give historic value. The stool claim is one of the premises behind it.

questions.stimulus: In surveys, patients in the Calloway health system named cost more often than any other reason for failing to refill their blood-pressure prescriptions on time. Yet after Calloway made its most widely prescribed blood-pressure drug free to its patients, the proportion of patients taking that drug who failed to refill it on time did not decline at all.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why making the drug free did not reduce the proportion of late refills?
choices: Fewer than half of the patients who reported failing to refill on time named cost as the main reason they had done so.
Patients usually fill all their prescriptions in one trip, which those short of money delay until they can afford the other drugs.
Patients who refill their blood-pressure prescriptions on time suffer fewer strokes than patients who do not.
The free drug is as effective as the more expensive blood-pressure drugs that Calloway’s physicians sometimes prescribe.
Some patients who fail to refill their prescriptions on time do so simply because they lose track of when each of their refills is due.
questions.explanation: If patients collect all their prescriptions in one visit and short-of-money patients put off that whole visit because of the other, still-costly drugs, then the free drug gets refilled late anyway, so cost still drives the delay; that is (B). (A) and (E) are tempting because they point to reasons other than cost, but as long as cost was the most common reason, removing it should have reduced late refills at least somewhat, and the puzzle is that they didn’t decline at all.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Cost was the top reason for late refills, but making the drug free didn’t reduce late refills of it at all.

breakdown.analysis: If cost is the main reason people refill late, why didn’t ‘free’ help even a little? Maybe the cost that matters isn’t this drug’s price. If patients buy everything in one trip, and the trip is still expensive because of the other drugs, then making one drug free doesn’t change when they show up. We need an answer that shows cost still blocks the refill even though this drug is free.

choices.note: Tempting, because it shrinks the cost group. But cost was still the most common reason. Removing it should have reduced late refills somewhat, and they didn’t decline at all.

CORRECT. The refill is tied to one pharmacy trip, and that trip still costs money because of the other drugs. Patients short of cash postpone the whole trip, so the free drug is refilled late just as before. Cost still explains the delay.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. It tells us why refilling on time matters, not why the free drug didn’t change behavior.
Effectiveness is a different dimension. It doesn’t explain anything about refill timing.
Tempting, since forgetting is another cause. But ‘some’ forget doesn’t explain why the cost group, the biggest group, didn’t improve.

questions.stimulus: Publisher: Over four decades, our press built its reputation on accuracy, and we should not put that reputation at risk. Dr. Ames’s history of Harrow Lake is lively and well organized, but it makes many claims about local families that no one has checked against public records. So we should not publish the book in its current form.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the publisher’s argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Publishing a book that contains factual errors would put the press’s long-standing reputation for accuracy at risk.
Most published histories of small communities contain at least some errors concerning local families.
The press should publish no book containing claims about local families unless those claims were checked against public records.
Any book whose claims about local families have been checked against public records is accurate enough for the press to publish.
Dr. Ames did not consult any public records at all while writing his history of Harrow Lake.
questions.explanation: The book contains claims about local families that haven’t been checked against public records; if checking such claims is required before publishing, the book can’t be published as is, so (C) guarantees the conclusion. (D) is the trap: it gives the sufficient-condition version, telling us when a book may be published, which says nothing about an unchecked one. (A) fails because unchecked claims aren’t shown to be errors.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The press should not publish Ames’s book in its current form.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The press shouldn’t risk its reputation for accuracy; the book has many claims about local families that haven’t been checked against public records.

breakdown.analysis: Unchecked isn’t the same as wrong. So how do we get from ‘unchecked claims’ to ‘don’t publish’? The cleanest bridge makes checking a requirement: publish → claims checked. The book’s claims weren’t checked, so by the contrapositive: not checked → don’t publish. Chain: book has unchecked family claims → (rule) → should not publish. Watch for the sufficient version of this rule; it points the wrong way.

choices.note: Tempting, because it ties into the reputation premise. But the book’s claims are unchecked, not shown to be false. Without knowing there are errors, this rule never kicks in.
‘Most histories’ having some errors makes errors likely, not certain, and still doesn’t say errors mean don’t publish. Not enough to force the conclusion.
CORRECT. Checking against public records is now a requirement for publication. The book fails it, so it shouldn’t be published as is.

Tempting, but it’s the wrong direction. It says when checked books may be published. It says nothing about what to do with an unchecked one. It’s the sufficient version of the needed necessary condition.
This explains why the claims are unchecked, which we already know. It still doesn’t tell us that unchecked means don’t publish.

questions.stimulus: Ten years ago, Belwick College ranked third among the state’s twelve liberal arts colleges in the percentage of its graduates who go on to graduate school, a figure the state’s college association publishes each year. This year it ranked seventh. Clearly, then, the millions of dollars that Belwick spent on its faculty-mentoring program during the past decade did not prevent that percentage at Belwick from declining.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: fails to consider that the mentoring program might provide benefits to Belwick’s students other than an increase in graduate-school enrollment
overlooks the possibility that the percentage at Belwick would have fallen even further had the mentoring program not been funded
presumes, without providing justification, that the state’s other colleges spent less on mentoring programs than Belwick spent
ignores the possibility that Belwick’s enrollment grew more slowly over the decade than did the enrollments of the other colleges
infers that Belwick’s own percentage of graduates going on to graduate school fell from a decline in how that percentage compares with other colleges’
questions.explanation: Falling from third to seventh shows only that more colleges now have higher percentages than Belwick; Belwick’s own percentage could have held steady or risen while others rose faster, and (E) names that relative-to-absolute slip. (B) is the dominant trap, but it describes a flaw the argument does not commit: the conclusion is only that the spending did not prevent a decline, which is true whenever a decline happened, even if things would have been worse without the program. (D) is irrelevant because the ranking is by percentage, which already adjusts for size.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The mentoring-program spending did not prevent the percentage of Belwick graduates going on to graduate school from declining.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Belwick fell from third to seventh of twelve colleges in the percentage of graduates who go on to graduate school.

breakdown.analysis: Did the percentage at Belwick actually go down? All we know is that its rank dropped, and rankings are relative. Picture it: Belwick goes from 30 percent to 34 percent while four other colleges jump from 25 to 40. Belwick slides to seventh while its own number grows. Moving down a ranking isn’t an absolute decrease; that’s a classic slip, know it. We need an answer that says the argument reads a lower rank as a lower percentage. Most students pick (B), because ‘it would have been even worse without the program’ is the textbook objection to any before-and-after argument about spending. It fails here because the conclusion is only that the program didn’t PREVENT a decline; if the percentage fell at all, that’s true whether or not it would have fallen further. The right answer (E) hides behind abstract wording: ‘how that percentage compares with other colleges’’ is just the ranking.

choices.note: So? The argument never says the program was worthless. It says only that it didn’t stop a decline. Other benefits don’t touch that.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The new stadium didn’t raise tax revenue, so it did the city no good at all.

choices.note: Tempting. It’s the standard counterfactual objection, and it sounds like the right criticism of an argument about spending. But read the conclusion: the spending ‘did not prevent’ a decline. If the percentage fell, the program didn’t prevent the fall, even if things would have been worse without it. The argument doesn’t need to deny (B), so (B) isn’t its flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Burglaries rose after we hired more officers, so hiring them made no difference to burglaries.

choices.note: Irrelevant. What other colleges spent has nothing to do with whether Belwick’s own percentage fell.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our school’s test scores beat Lakeside’s, so our school must spend more per student.

choices.note: The ranking is by percentage of graduates, which already adjusts for college size. How fast enrollment grew explains nothing here.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our town has more car accidents than the village next door, so our drivers are worse.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘How that percentage compares with other colleges’’ is the ranking. The argument infers that Belwick’s own percentage fell from the fact that its rank fell, but the rank can drop while the percentage holds steady or rises.

questions.stimulus: Sociologist: Some attribute the decline of neighborhood bowling leagues to longer working hours. If that were right, league membership should have fallen most among people whose working hours grew the most. Yet over the past two decades membership fell fastest among retirees, whose working hours did not grow at all, while it fell least among people working long shifts. So longer hours are unlikely to be the main cause of the decline.
questions.stem: The sociologist’s argument proceeds by
choices: offering an alternative explanation for a decline and arguing that it fits the available evidence better than a rival explanation does
pointing out that an explanation under consideration implies a pattern in the evidence markedly different from the pattern actually observed
arguing that because a proposed cause did not affect one group, that cause could not have affected any group at all
showing that the proposed cause was absent in every group in which league membership declined over the past two decades
questioning the reliability of the data on working hours on which a rival explanation of a decline is based
questions.explanation: The sociologist draws a prediction from the working-hours explanation (the biggest drop where hours grew most) and shows the evidence runs the other way (the biggest drop among retirees, the smallest among long-shift workers); that is (B). (A) is the trap: the sociologist rejects one explanation but never proposes another. (C) overstates the conclusion, which says only that longer hours are unlikely to be the main cause, and (D) is false, since people working long shifts also declined.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Longer working hours are unlikely to be the main cause of the decline in bowling leagues.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: If longer hours were the cause, membership should have fallen most where hours grew most; instead it fell fastest among retirees and least among long-shift workers.

breakdown.analysis: Describe the moves, not the topic. Move 1: take the rival explanation and ask what it predicts (“should have fallen most among…”). Move 2: show the evidence does the opposite. Move 3: conclude the explanation probably isn’t the main cause. That is testing an explanation by its consequences. Notice what the sociologist doesn’t do: there is no alternative cause anywhere, and the conclusion is hedged (“unlikely,” “main”). Answers that add a rival theory or inflate the conclusion are traps.

choices.note: Tempting, because rejecting one explanation usually comes with a replacement. Not here. The sociologist never says what did cause the decline.
choices.example: Example of this method: Longer hours don’t explain the decline as well as the rise of home entertainment does, which fits every group’s numbers.

choices.note: CORRECT. The working-hours explanation implies the biggest drop where hours grew most. The data show the biggest drop where hours didn’t grow at all, and the smallest among long-shift workers. The mismatch is the whole argument.
Too strong. The sociologist says longer hours are unlikely to be the main cause, not that they had no effect on anyone. And the evidence is a pattern across groups, not one group.
choices.example: Example of this method: Longer hours didn’t affect retirees, so they didn’t affect anyone’s league membership.

choices.note: False to the stimulus. Membership also fell among people working long shifts, who presumably did have longer hours. The argument relies on the pattern of the declines, not on the cause being absent everywhere.
choices.example: Example of this method: Every group whose membership fell had unchanged working hours, so hours can’t be the cause.

choices.note: The sociologist accepts the data and uses them. Nothing questions how working hours were measured.
choices.example: Example of this method: The surveys of working hours were self-reported, so the explanation built on them is unreliable.

questions.stimulus: Three years ago, the town of Fairhope planted a continuous row of shade trees along Bram Street, its main shopping street. Since then, the number of pedestrians using Bram Street on summer afternoons has risen by about a quarter. Evidently, the shade has made walking on Bram Street more appealing to people in hot weather.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the argument EXCEPT:
choices: On nearby Tull Street, a similar shopping street with no shade trees, summer-afternoon pedestrian counts have not changed in three years.
Sidewalk temperatures on Bram Street on summer afternoons are now markedly lower than they were before the trees were planted.
On overcast summer afternoons, pedestrian counts on Bram Street have risen by about as much as they have on sunny summer afternoons.
Many people surveyed on Bram Street on hot afternoons said they chose it over nearby streets because it felt cooler.
The rise in summer-afternoon pedestrians began the first summer after the trees were planted, before any of Bram Street’s new shops had opened.
questions.explanation: The argument credits the shade. Shade matters on sunny afternoons, not overcast ones, when clouds already block the sun. If counts rose just as much on overcast afternoons, something other than shade is drawing people; (C) weakens rather than strengthens, so it is the exception. (E) is the trap: it mentions new shops, which sounds like an alternative cause, but it actually strengthens the argument by showing the rise began before any shops opened. (A), (B), and (D) each strengthen.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The shade trees made Bram Street more appealing to walkers in hot weather.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Trees were planted three years ago; summer-afternoon pedestrian counts have since risen about 25 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Four answers help the shade story; one doesn’t. Ways to help: a comparison street without trees that didn’t change, proof the trees really cool the street, people saying they came for the coolness, timing that rules out another cause. So which one hurts? Ask when shade should matter. On an overcast afternoon the trees add little, so a shade effect predicts a bigger rise on sunny afternoons than on cloudy ones. Equal rises point to some other cause. Most students hunt for an obvious alternative cause, find “new shops” in (E), and pick it. Read (E) again: the rise started before the shops opened, which helps the argument.

choices.note: Strengthens. A similar street without trees saw no change, so the rise on Bram Street isn’t just a town-wide trend.
Strengthens. It confirms the mechanism: the trees really do make the street cooler on summer afternoons.
CORRECT. This is the exception. When it’s overcast, shade from the trees makes little difference. If counts rose just as much then, the rise isn’t explained by shade, which weakens the argument.
Strengthens. People report choosing the street because it felt cooler, which is what the shade is supposed to do.
Tempting, because “new shops” look like a rival cause. But the rise began before any of them opened, which rules the shops out as the original cause and ties the rise to the trees. It strengthens.

questions.stimulus: Each spring the frogs of Harlan Pond begin their mating calls within two days of the same calendar date, even though the date on which the pond’s ice melts varies by as much as three weeks from one year to the next. Since the frogs’ start date does not track the melting of the ice, the frogs must be timing their calls chiefly by an internal clock rather than by a seasonal cue from their surroundings.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Any frog population that times its mating calls by an internal clock starts calling within a few days of the same date every year.
Frogs in ponds where the ice melts at about the same time each year also begin calling on a consistent date each spring.
The temperature of the water in Harlan Pond plays no role at all in determining the date on which the frogs begin calling.
Nothing in the pond or its surroundings that the frogs are able to detect changes on nearly the same date each spring.
The date on which Harlan Pond’s ice melts has no influence on when the pond’s frogs lay their eggs.
questions.explanation: The argument rules out the ice as a cue and then concludes that the frogs rely chiefly on an internal clock rather than on any seasonal cue. That leap requires that nothing detectable in the surroundings changes on a fixed date each year, because such a feature (day length, for instance) could produce a fixed calling date with no internal clock; that is (D). (C) is the dominant trap, but it is too strong: the conclusion says “chiefly,” so water temperature could nudge the date within the two-day window while a clock does the main timing. (A) reverses the reasoning, which runs from a fixed date to a clock, not from a clock to a fixed date.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The frogs time their calls chiefly by an internal clock, not by a seasonal cue from their surroundings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The frogs start calling within two days of the same date every year; the ice-melt date varies by up to three weeks, so the calls don’t track the ice.

breakdown.analysis: So the frogs ignore the ice. Does that mean they rely chiefly on something inside them? Only if the ice was the only seasonal cue on offer. What about something in the surroundings that changes on the same date every year, like the length of the day? A cue like that would give a fixed calling date with no internal clock at all. The argument eliminated one outside cue and treated all of them as gone. We need an answer that says there is no detectable outside cue running on a fixed yearly schedule. Most students pick (C), because temperature feels like exactly the outside cue the argument is ruling out. It fails because ‘no role at all’ is too strong: the conclusion only says the clock is the chief timer, so warm or cold water could shift the date by a day, which even fits the two-day spread. The right answer (D) hides as a vague claim about ‘nothing in the surroundings,’ but it is the precondition the whole elimination step rests on.

choices.note: This reverses the reasoning. The argument goes from ‘same date every year’ to ‘internal clock,’ not from ‘clock’ to ‘same date.’ Negate it and some clock-timed frogs vary their dates. So? The Harlan Pond frogs don’t vary, and the argument says nothing about other populations.
choices.negation: Some frog populations that time their calls by an internal clock start calling on dates that vary widely from year to year.

choices.note: Interesting, but not required. Other ponds tell us nothing about which cue the Harlan Pond frogs use. Negating it doesn’t touch the argument.
choices.negation: In some ponds where the ice melts at about the same time each year, the frogs do not begin calling on a consistent date.

choices.note: Tempting. Temperature is the obvious outside cue, so ruling it out feels required. But this is too strong. Negate it: water temperature plays some role. The conclusion only says the clock is the chief timer, so a warm or cold spell can move the date by a day and the argument survives. (C) isn’t required.
choices.negation: The temperature of the water in Harlan Pond plays some role in determining when the frogs begin calling.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: something the frogs can detect, such as day length, changes on nearly the same date every spring. Then that cue could be what chiefly sets the fixed calling date, and the inference to an internal clock collapses.
choices.negation: Something in the pond or its surroundings that the frogs can detect does change on nearly the same date each spring.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Egg laying is a different event. The argument is only about when the frogs start calling.
choices.negation: The date on which the pond’s ice melts has some influence on when the frogs lay their eggs.

questions.stimulus: Every applicant who is offered a residency at a certain arts colony has submitted a portfolio that was reviewed by at least two jurors. Most of this year’s applicants from the city’s design school had their portfolios reviewed by two or more jurors. So most of this year’s applicants from the design school will be offered residencies.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Every nurse at the clinic who has completed the advanced triage course is qualified to supervise a ward. Most of the nurses hired in 2015 have completed that course. So most of them are qualified to supervise a ward.

Every cook who has trained in Lyon is offered a post at the restaurant. Most of this year’s new cooks have not trained in Lyon. So most of this year’s new cooks will not be offered a post at the restaurant.

No one is promoted to senior editor at the magazine without first having worked on at least three cover stories. Most of the staff writers hired in 2015 have worked on three or more. So most of them will be promoted to senior editor.

Every player chosen for the regional team attended the summer training camp, and most of the camp’s attendees came from the city. So most of the players chosen for the regional team came from the city.

Most of the musicians who audition for the orchestra have studied at a conservatory, and every musician who studies at a conservatory learns to sight-read. So most of the musicians who audition for the orchestra can sight-read.
questions.explanation: The argument treats a necessary condition as sufficient and applies it to “most” of a group: offered → reviewed by two jurors; most design applicants were reviewed by two; so most will be offered. (C) does the same once “no one is promoted without” is translated: promoted → three cover stories; most 2015 hires have three; so most will be promoted. (A) is the dominant trap: its “every … most … most” shape lines up with the original on the surface, but its rule makes the triage course sufficient for qualifying, so it is valid. (B) negates the sufficient condition, (D) chains “every” with “most” the wrong way, and (E) is a valid “most … every” chain.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most of this year’s design-school applicants will be offered residencies.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every applicant offered a residency had a portfolio reviewed by at least two jurors; most design-school applicants had two or more reviewers.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Every A is B (A → B). Most C are B. So most C are A. (Treats the necessary condition B as sufficient.)

breakdown.analysis: Two jurors is required for an offer, not a guarantee of one. Lots of twice-reviewed portfolios could be turned down. It’s like saying every Olympian trained daily, most of my club trains daily, so most of my club will make the Olympics. Translate every choice into arrows and check three things: which side of the arrow the group satisfies, whether the quantifiers are “every … most … most,” and whether the conclusion is the same kind of claim. Every wrong answer here keeps most of the surface and changes one of those. Most students pick (A), because it opens with “Every …,” uses “most” twice and ends on a prediction-like “most of them are …,” just like the original. But (A)’s rule runs the other way: course → qualified. Satisfying a sufficient condition proves the result, so (A) is valid. (C) hides its rule in “no one is promoted without,” which means promoted → three stories.

choices.note: Tempting, because its sentences line up one for one with the original’s. But its rule is triage course → qualified, a sufficient condition. Most nurses meet it, so most are qualified. That’s valid; the original is flawed.

A different error. Trained in Lyon → offered; most didn’t train in Lyon; so most won’t be offered. That negates the sufficient condition rather than affirming the necessary one. Flawed, but not the same flaw.

CORRECT. “No one is promoted without three cover stories” means promoted → three stories. Most 2015 hires have three stories, and the argument concludes most will be promoted. Same move: a necessary condition treated as sufficient, applied to “most.”

A different flaw. Every A is B and most B are C, so most A are C. The team players could all come from the minority of attendees who weren’t from the city. It’s a quantifier error, not a necessary-sufficient error.
Valid chain: most auditioners studied at a conservatory, and every conservatory student sight-reads, so most auditioners sight-read. The original is flawed, so a valid argument can’t match.

questions.stimulus: Labor mediator: The Oriel Hotel’s management wants to require its housekeepers to wear location-tracking badges throughout their shifts, saying the data would help it schedule cleaning more efficiently. But the same scheduling gains could be achieved by having housekeepers log each room as they finish it, which would reveal far less about their movements. So the hotel should not adopt the badge requirement.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the labor mediator’s argument?
choices: An employer should not adopt a practice that employees find intrusive if the practice would yield no gain in efficiency.
An employer is not justified in gathering information about its employees beyond what it needs in order to achieve its legitimate aims.
An employer should not adopt a monitoring practice if a less intrusive alternative would cost less to put into effect.
If a workplace practice would make operations more efficient without intruding on employees’ privacy, an employer should adopt it.
An employer should not adopt a practice if the purpose it states for the practice differs from the purpose it would actually serve.
questions.explanation: The mediator’s point is that room logs would deliver the same scheduling gains while revealing far less about housekeepers’ movements, so the badges would collect more than the hotel’s purpose needs. (B) forbids gathering information beyond what a legitimate aim requires, which yields the conclusion. (A) and (C) have the right verdict but conditions the stimulus doesn’t meet: the badges would produce efficiency gains, and nothing is said about cost. (D) supports adopting the logs, not rejecting the badges.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The hotel should not adopt the badge requirement.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The badges would serve scheduling efficiency; room logs would achieve the same gains while revealing far less about housekeepers’ movements.

breakdown.analysis: Why is the mediator against the badges? Not because scheduling is a bad goal; the mediator accepts it. The objection is that the badges collect more than the goal requires, since logs would do the same job. So we need a principle saying: don’t collect more about employees than your purpose needs. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, and its condition has to be met by the facts. Several answers here reach “should not adopt” but hang it on a condition the stimulus never satisfies.

choices.note: Tempting, because it has the right verdict and the word “intrusive.” But its condition is that the practice yields no efficiency gain, and the badges would yield gains. The mediator’s complaint is that the gains could be had another way.
CORRECT. The badges would gather movement data beyond what scheduling requires, since logs achieve the same gains. A legitimate aim, more information than needed: not justified.
Right verdict, wrong condition. The mediator never mentions cost. We don’t know whether the logs are cheaper, so this principle never kicks in.
This would tell the hotel to adopt the room logs. It says nothing about whether to reject the badges.
The mediator never questions the hotel’s stated purpose. This answer imports a cynical story the argument doesn’t tell.

questions.stimulus: The mineral orvanite forms only where molten volcanic rock comes into contact with seawater. Once exposed to air, orvanite breaks down completely within two thousand years. Last year a landslide in the Eskar Highlands, a region far from any present-day coast, sheared away the face of a cliff, and the newly exposed rock was found to contain abundant orvanite.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The orvanite in the Eskar Highlands cliff must have formed at some time within the last two thousand years.
Any rock in the Eskar Highlands that has been exposed to air for several centuries contains no orvanite.
The site of the Eskar Highlands cliff was in contact with the sea at some time within the past two thousand years.
Most of the orvanite that has formed anywhere on Earth has since broken down completely as a result of exposure to air.
Either the cliff’s orvanite formed elsewhere and was later moved, or seawater once reached the place where the cliff now stands.
questions.explanation: Orvanite forms only where molten rock meets seawater, and the cliff’s orvanite sits far from any coast. So either it formed elsewhere and was carried here, or the sea once reached this spot; (E) says exactly that. (A) is the dominant trap: it treats the two-thousand-year breakdown as a limit on the orvanite’s age, but the limit applies only to exposure to air, and the orvanite was buried until last year. (C) builds on the same mistake.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Orvanite forms only where molten volcanic rock meets seawater; 2. orvanite exposed to air breaks down completely within two thousand years; 3. the Eskar Highlands are far from any present-day coast; 4. a landslide last year exposed cliff rock full of orvanite.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so ask what each fact forces. Fact 1 plus the orvanite in the cliff: molten rock met seawater wherever this orvanite formed. Fact 3: there’s no sea near the Highlands now. So either the orvanite formed somewhere else and got moved, or the sea used to be here. Fact 2 is the bait. It limits how long orvanite survives in air, not how old it can be. This orvanite was sealed inside the cliff until last year, so it could be millions of years old. Most students pick (A) because “two thousand years” jumps out. The right answer hides as an “either…or” that looks too cautious to be interesting.

choices.note: Tempting, because it uses the two-thousand-year figure. But that figure is about exposure to air. This orvanite was inside the cliff until the landslide, so nothing limits its age.
Too quick. Orvanite lasts up to two thousand years in air, so rock exposed for a few centuries could still hold some. “Several centuries” isn’t long enough to guarantee it’s gone.
This builds on the same mistake as (A). We know seawater met molten rock wherever the orvanite formed, but nothing dates that event, and the orvanite might have formed elsewhere.
Unsupported generalization. The facts tell us what happens to exposed orvanite, not how much of the world’s orvanite has ever been exposed.

CORRECT. Orvanite forms only where molten rock meets seawater. The cliff is far from any present coast, so either the orvanite formed elsewhere and was later moved, or seawater once reached the cliff’s site. One of the two must hold.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: Many clay oil lamps from the ancient town of Ithane have a small hole pierced through the handle. The hole was not needed for the lamp to burn, since many lamps without it are heavily sooted from long use. But a far greater proportion of the lamps found in the town’s shrines have the hole than of those found in its houses. So the hole most likely let lamps be hung on shrine walls during rituals.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the archaeologist’s argument?
choices: More lamps in all were found in the town’s shrines than were found in all of the town’s houses combined.
Lamps hung from cords or pegs played a part in the religious rituals of several other ancient peoples of the region.
Lamps without the hole show signs of having been burned for at least as long as lamps that have the hole.
Lamps found in the town’s shrines were, on average, larger and more elaborately decorated than lamps found in its houses.
Between festivals, the town’s shrines stored hundreds of lamps at a time by sliding them onto wooden rods through their handles.
questions.explanation: The argument infers the hole’s purpose from its being more common in shrine lamps. If shrines had to store hundreds of lamps between festivals by threading them onto rods, the hole served shrine storage rather than hanging during rituals, which explains the shrine–hole link with no wall-hanging at all; that is (E). (A) is the dominant trap: more lamps in shrines would explain more holed lamps there, but the argument is about proportions, which a larger total doesn’t affect. (B) strengthens, (C) merely confirms a premise, and (D) names a difference that does nothing to explain the holes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The hole in the lamp handles most likely let lamps be hung on shrine walls during rituals.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The hole wasn’t needed for burning; a far greater proportion of shrine lamps than house lamps have it.

breakdown.analysis: The evidence is a correlation: holes go with shrines. Does that show the hole was for hanging lamps on shrine walls during rituals? Only if nothing else about shrines would call for a hole in the handle. What else could? Shrines differ from houses in more than rituals. A shrine that had to keep hundreds of lamps between festivals needs a way to store them, and a household with a few lamps doesn’t. If the hole was for threading lamps onto storage rods, the shrine–hole link is explained with no wall-hanging at all. Most students pick (A), because “more lamps in shrines” sounds like it explains “more holed lamps in shrines.” It fails because the archaeologist compares proportions, and a bigger pile of lamps doesn’t change a proportion. The right answer hides because it looks like trivia about storage until you see that it gives the hole a different shrine-specific job.

choices.note: Tempting. It looks like it explains away the shrine numbers. But the archaeologist compares proportions: a larger share of shrine lamps have the hole. How many lamps each place held doesn’t touch a proportion. This is a count-versus-rate trap.
This helps the archaeologist. If neighbors hung lamps in rituals, a hanging hole for ritual use is more plausible.
This just repeats what the argument already says: lamps without the hole were used for a long time. Confirming a premise doesn’t weaken anything.
Tempting, because it shows shrine lamps were a special kind of lamp. But size and decoration don’t explain why shrine lamps more often have a hole. Nothing here gives the hole another job.

CORRECT. Shrines needed to store many lamps; threading them on rods through the handle requires a hole; houses with a few lamps didn’t need that. So the shrine–hole link is explained by storage, not by hanging lamps on walls during rituals.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacist: A prescription for a drug in the restricted category can be refilled without a new consultation only if the prescribing physician has signed a long-term-use authorization for that patient within the past year. Dr. Hale, who prescribes Velacor for Mr. Ruiz, signs such authorizations only during in-person examinations, and she has not examined Mr. Ruiz in person in more than two years. So Velacor must not be in the restricted category.
questions.stem: The pharmacist’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Dr. Hale has not signed a long-term-use authorization for Mr. Ruiz at any time within the past year.
Any drug for which a prescription can properly be refilled without a new consultation falls outside the restricted category.
Mr. Ruiz’s prescription for Velacor was refilled last week, in full compliance with the rules, without a new consultation.
If Dr. Hale had examined Mr. Ruiz in person within the past year, she would have signed an authorization for his Velacor.
Some of Dr. Hale’s other patients have had their prescriptions for Velacor refilled without a new consultation.
questions.explanation: The premises show that Mr. Ruiz has no authorization from the past year, so if Velacor were restricted, his prescription could not properly be refilled without a new consultation. (C) says it was properly refilled that way, so Velacor cannot be restricted. (B) is the dominant trap: it looks like the conditional bridge a sufficient-assumption answer usually supplies, but nothing establishes that a Velacor prescription can be refilled without a consultation, so its condition is never triggered. (A) only restates what the premises already establish.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Velacor is not in the restricted category.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Restricted drug refilled without a new consultation → prescriber signed an authorization within the past year; Hale signs only during in-person exams; she hasn’t examined Ruiz in over two years.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Hale hasn’t examined Ruiz in two years and signs only during exams → no authorization in the past year. Restricted AND refilled without consultation → authorization in the past year. Put together: if Velacor is restricted, Ruiz can’t be refilled without a consultation. So far the premises only say what WOULD happen if Velacor were restricted. To prove it isn’t, we need the other half: Ruiz did get a proper refill without a consultation. Refilled + no authorization → not restricted. Most students pick (B), because sufficient-assumption answers are usually ‘any X is Y’ bridges and (B) uses the right words. It fails because its trigger, a prescription that can be refilled without a consultation, is never shown for Velacor; the premises point the other way. The right answer (C) hides because it’s a plain fact, not a rule.

choices.note: Already established. Hale signs only in person and hasn’t seen Ruiz in two years, so we know this. Repeating it adds nothing, and the conclusion still doesn’t follow.
Tempting. It looks like the bridge you expect. But it helps only if some Velacor prescription can properly be refilled without a consultation, and nothing says so. Its condition never gets triggered.
CORRECT. A proper refill without a consultation, with no authorization from the past year, is impossible for a restricted drug. So Velacor isn’t restricted.
