So? What Hale would have done after a hypothetical exam tells us nothing about which category Velacor is in.
Other patients may have recent authorizations from in-person exams. Their refills fit perfectly well with Velacor being restricted, so this proves nothing.

questions.stimulus: Consumer advocate: Roofing firms account for a larger share of the complaints about home contractors filed with Dalby’s consumer office than any other kind of contractor does. Admittedly, some complaints are unjustified, and many homeowners with good cause never file one, but neither tendency is more common among roofing customers than among others. So a Dalby homeowner who hires a roofing firm is more likely to end up with good cause for complaint than one who hires any other kind of contractor.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the consumer advocate’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that some roofing firms in Dalby may draw far more complaints than other roofing firms do
presumes, without providing justification, that roofing firms do not handle an even larger share of the contracting jobs in Dalby
fails to consider that roofing jobs might give homeowners good cause for complaint more often than other kinds of jobs do
overlooks the possibility that complaints about roofing firms are resolved to the homeowner’s satisfaction more often than other complaints are
confuses how likely a homeowner is to file a complaint with how likely that homeowner is to have good cause for one
questions.explanation: “Share of the complaints” sounds like a rate, but it is a share of a total, not a share of jobs. If roofing firms handle an even larger share of Dalby’s contracting jobs than of its complaints, a roofing job is less likely than average to lead to trouble; the argument simply presumes otherwise, as (B) says. (E) is the sophisticated trap: it names a real worry about complaint data, but the advocate concedes that unjustified and unfiled complaints exist and argues that neither is more common among roofing customers. (A) and (D) raise possibilities the argument never addresses, but neither matters: the conclusion is about the average roofing hire, so variation among roofers is beside the point, and how complaints get resolved says nothing about whether there was good cause to file them. (C) describes something that would support the conclusion, not a flaw.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A Dalby homeowner who hires a roofing firm is more likely to end up with good cause for complaint than one who hires any other kind of contractor.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Roofing firms draw a larger share of complaints than any other kind of contractor; unjustified and unfiled complaints are no more common among roofing customers than among others.

breakdown.analysis: A larger share of the complaints: does that mean a roofing job is more likely to go wrong? Only if roofers don’t also do a larger share of the jobs. Imagine roofers do 50 percent of Dalby’s jobs and draw 40 percent of the complaints. They lead the complaint list, yet each roofing job is less likely than average to cause trouble. The word “share” disguises a total as a rate; know this one. The advocate is careful about the filing side: the concession sentence heads off objections about unjustified and unfiled complaints, so (E) is a trap. Other choices raise things the advocate really doesn’t mention, but an unaddressed possibility is a flaw only if it would undercut the conclusion. The right answer hides in an oddly specific phrase, “an even larger share of the contracting jobs,” which is exactly the missing comparison.

choices.note: True, the argument never mentions differences among roofers. So? The conclusion is about a homeowner who hires a roofing firm, which is an average over roofers. A few bad firms dragging up the count doesn’t make the average roofing hire any safer, so this doesn’t touch the reasoning.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our town’s restaurants draw few health complaints, so every restaurant in town must be clean.

choices.note: CORRECT. If roofers do an even larger share of the jobs than of the complaints, their complaint rate per job is below average. The advocate moves from a share of complaints to a likelihood per hire without ruling that out.
This uses the argument’s own words in the wrong relation. If roofing jobs did cause trouble more often, the conclusion would be true. Failing to consider a possibility that supports you isn’t a flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The data show roofers draw few complaints, so roofing must be the safest hire, never mind that roofing jobs might go wrong more often.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The conclusion is about having good cause for a complaint, not about how complaints end. A roofer who fixes the leak after the homeowner complains still gave good cause to complain. The argument doesn’t need to say anything about resolution.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most complaints about the cable company are resolved within a week, so its customers rarely have reason to complain.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a sophisticated version of the right idea. But the advocate addresses exactly this gap: filing and having good cause come apart in the same ways for roofing customers as for everyone else.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: More people complain about airlines than about trains, so airline passengers must have more reason to complain.

questions.stimulus: Harbor rules allow a vessel to enter the harbor after dark only if a licensed pilot is aboard, except for fishing boats registered in the port. The cargo ship Medra, which is registered in another port, has no licensed pilot aboard tonight. So the Medra may not enter the harbor after dark tonight.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: A student may enroll in the advanced seminar only if she has completed the introductory course, unless she has the instructor’s written permission. Tomas has not completed the introductory course. So Tomas may not enroll in the advanced seminar.

A student who has completed the introductory course may enroll in the advanced seminar, unless the seminar is already full. Lena has not completed the introductory course, and the seminar is not full. So Lena may not enroll in the seminar.

Priya may not enroll in the advanced seminar. After all, she has neither completed the introductory course nor obtained the instructor’s written permission, and the seminar admits only those who have completed that course, apart from students with such permission.

Library rules allow a patron to borrow a rare book only if she holds a research card, except for members of the university faculty. Mara, a visiting scholar who is not on the faculty, holds a research card. So Mara may borrow a rare book.

The advanced seminar admits only students who have completed the introductory course, apart from those with the instructor’s written permission. Jae has completed that course but has not obtained such permission. So Jae may not enroll in the advanced seminar.
questions.explanation: The argument is valid: a vessel may enter after dark only if it has a pilot or is an exempt fishing boat; the Medra has neither; so it may not enter. (C) has the same shape with its conclusion first: Priya has neither the course nor the permission, so she may not enroll. (A) is the dominant trap: it checks only the main condition and never rules out the exception. (E) uses the same rule but treats the exception as an extra requirement: Jae meets the main condition, so lacking permission doesn’t bar him. (B) negates a sufficient condition, and (D) treats a necessary condition as sufficient.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Medra may not enter the harbor after dark tonight.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A vessel may enter after dark only if a pilot is aboard, except fishing boats registered here; the Medra is not a registered fishing boat and has no pilot.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Permitted → X or exempt. Not X and not exempt. So not permitted. (Valid.)

breakdown.analysis: Diagram the rule with its exception: may enter → pilot aboard OR registered fishing boat. The Medra fails both, so it may not enter. Valid. Now check each choice for three things: the rule and its exception, both conditions ruled out, and a conclusion about what is permitted. Every wrong answer misses at least one. Most students pick (A), because its rule matches word for word; but it never rules out the exception, so Tomas might have permission. Others pick (E), which copies (C)’s rule and denies the permission, but Jae has completed the course, so he satisfies the rule; (E) treats the exemption as a second requirement. (C) hides by stating its conclusion first and its rule last.

choices.note: Tempting, because the rule is a perfect match, exception and all. But the argument rules out only the main condition. Tomas might have the instructor’s permission, so the conclusion doesn’t follow. The original rules out both.
This turns a sufficient condition into a requirement. Completing the course is enough to enroll (if there’s room), but nothing says it’s needed. Flawed where the original is valid.
CORRECT. Rule: admitted → completed the course OR has permission. Priya has neither, so she may not enroll. Same valid shape, with the conclusion moved to the front.

Different logic. A research card is required, not a guarantee, so having one doesn’t show Mara may borrow. It treats a necessary condition as sufficient, and its conclusion says what is allowed rather than what is barred.

Tempting, because it has the same rule as (C) and denies the permission. But Jae has completed the course, which satisfies the main condition: admitted → course OR permission, and he has the course. Nothing bars him. The argument treats an exemption as an extra requirement. The original denies both routes; this denies only the backup route.

passages.title: Cunningham, Cage, and the independence of dance and music
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
For most of the history of Western theatrical dance, choreography has been made to music: the choreographer begins with a score, and the dancers’ steps answer its meter, its phrasing, and its swells. The collaboration between the choreographer Merce Cunningham and the composer John Cage, which began in the 1940s and lasted until Cage’s death in 1992, abandoned that arrangement. In most of the works that Cunningham’s company performed, dance and music were made separately, and the dancers often heard the score for the first time at or shortly before the first performance.

Some early reviewers took this independence as a sign of indifference, reasoning that if the dance does not follow the music, the pairing of a particular dance with a particular score must be arbitrary, and either could be exchanged for another without loss. The working method was in fact quite deliberate. In the solo works Cunningham presented with Cage’s music in the mid-1940s, the two agreed in advance on a structure of time—a work’s overall length and its division into parts of fixed proportions—and then composed separately within it, so that dance and music, each going its own way, coincided at the boundaries between parts. Cage held that duration, rather than melody or harmony, is the one property that sound shares with silence, and a structure built of durations could be shared by movement as readily as by sound.

From the early 1950s Cunningham used chance procedures, such as tossing coins, to determine the order of phrases, the number of dancers, or the direction of a movement, and in many later works the common structure shrank to a single agreement about total length. Even then, the separation was not a refusal to relate the two arts but a way of leaving their relation open. Because neither was made to fit the other, any moment at which a sound and a gesture seemed to answer each other belonged to that performance alone: a crash in the score might coincide with a fall one night and with stillness the next. Cunningham rejected the convention that one point on the stage is more important than the others, leaving spectators to decide where to look; the independence of dance and music extended the same freedom to what they would hear.

The score also bore on what audiences saw, though less obviously. A dancer who has learned a phrase in silence must, once the score is added, hold to the phrase’s timing while sound that does not accompany it fills the theater. The music thus acts on the dance not as a guide but as a pressure, and the steadiness that resists it becomes part of what the audience sees.

passages.title: Kenning and Depression-era stamp scrip
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
In 1932 and 1933, with banks failing and cash scarce, many American towns and counties paid their employees partly in scrip: paper certificates that local merchants agreed to accept for goods and that the issuing government would take back in payment of taxes. Some of these issues followed a design promoted by the economist Irving Fisher. A one-dollar certificate carried fifty-two squares on its back, and to keep it valid its holder had to affix a two-cent stamp, bought from the issuer, to the next empty square each week; after a year the stamps had raised $1.04, enough to redeem the certificate. In a recent study, the economic historian Rhoda Kenning argues that this weekly charge, by making scrip costly to hold, induced people to spend it quickly, and that the resulting acceleration of exchange explains the revival of trade in the small mill town at the center of her study, which began issuing stamp scrip in the autumn of 1932, with both of its mills shut and its only bank closed.

Kenning’s account has the merit of attending to the design of a currency rather than merely to its quantity, and her reconstruction of the scrip’s movements from surviving stamp records is ingenious; the stamps may well have quickened trade as she says. What her evidence shows is less clear, beginning with what she takes the revival to consist in. At times she points to the number of transactions merchants recorded, at others to the total value of their sales. The number of transactions could rise while total sales stagnated, if residents merely broke their purchases into smaller ones to pass on scrip before the next stamp came due.

Her argument also assumes that merchants passed scrip on as readily as residents did. Her own figures suggest otherwise: most certificates came back to the town treasury within a few weeks, tendered by merchants in payment of property taxes. If the scrip traveled mainly from town employees to shopkeepers and back to the treasury, it may have functioned less as a circulating currency than as a means by which the town paid its workers out of future tax receipts—a useful arrangement, but not one that the stamps were needed to produce.

Finally, Kenning does not adequately address a neighboring town that issued scrip in 1933 without any stamp requirement and whose retail sales recovered at roughly the same rate. Kenning dismisses the comparison because the neighbor’s economy depended on a railway repair shop that reopened that year. But such a reopening could have contributed to her town’s recovery as well, since one of its mills resumed partial operation in the summer of 1933. A reason for discounting the neighbor’s recovery is equally a reason for discounting her own town’s.

passages.title: Apology statutes
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Passage A

Many jurisdictions have adopted apology statutes, which prevent a person’s expression of sympathy after an accident or injury from being introduced as evidence of liability in a later lawsuit. Their rationale is straightforward: people would apologize more readily if they did not fear that their words would be used against them, and injured parties who receive apologies would be less inclined to sue. Widely praised, the statutes rest on uncertain ground.

First, most of them protect only expressions of sympathy (“I am sorry this happened to you”) while leaving admissions of fault fully admissible. They thus encourage precisely the kind of apology that injured people find least satisfying: one that acknowledges suffering but sidesteps responsibility. Such a gesture gives injured people little or nothing of what they seek, and it may leave them feeling that their injury has been noted rather than answered.

Second, the statutes assume that fear of litigation is what keeps people from apologizing. But when the legal scholar Teodor Brann asked hospital physicians why they had not apologized after a medical error, they cited embarrassment, uncertainty about what had gone wrong, and institutional habit at least as often as legal exposure. A rule of evidence can do nothing about these.

Third, and most troubling, the statutes invite strategy. An insurer that coaches its policyholders to offer carefully worded, legally weightless expressions of regret may thereby defuse claims that deserve to be pursued, since an injured person who has been soothed is less likely to consult a lawyer. What was meant to make room for moral repair becomes one more instrument for managing liability.

Passage B

Evidence law has long excluded statements whose power to persuade a jury outruns their value as proof, and an expression of sympathy is a clear case. Jurors tend to hear “I’m sorry” as “It was my fault,” yet people routinely apologize for harms they did not cause: the host whose guest trips on a dry stair, the driver struck from behind. Laws keeping such statements from juries are therefore defensible on ordinary evidentiary grounds, whatever their effect on how often people apologize.

That effect is likely to be real. Fear of litigation may be only one of several reasons people withhold apologies, but removing one deterrent still leaves fewer in place, and a law need not cure a problem to be worth having.

Nor are the apologies such laws encourage empty. Granted, a protected statement of sympathy is not a confession of fault, and some injured people want the latter. A full apology might do more. But some studies of settlement negotiations suggest that even an acknowledgment admitting no fault can make some claimants more receptive to an offer. For many injured people, what matters first is that the harm be acknowledged. Critics who suspect every protected apology, as if regret could be sincere only when it is costly, confuse a statement’s legal consequences with the state of mind of the person who makes it.

passages.title: Crab cues and periwinkle shells in the Gulf of Maine
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
In the Gulf of Maine, the flat periwinkle, a small snail that lives on rockweed, varies strikingly in shell thickness. Snails from the southern gulf have thicker shells than northern ones, and shells collected at southern sites in the late nineteenth century are thinner than those gathered there a century later. Both patterns track the history of a predator. The European green crab arrived on the Atlantic coast of North America early in the nineteenth century but spread northward through the gulf only gradually during the twentieth, so that southern snails have lived alongside it far longer than northern ones.

The first explanation offered was evolutionary. Crabs, on this view, killed thin-shelled snails more readily than thick-shelled ones, and because the flat periwinkle lays its eggs on seaweed and its young crawl away rather than drifting as larvae, populations exposed to crabs could have diverged genetically from others within relatively few generations. The case was widely cited as natural selection observed within decades. But it rested on an assumption that had not been tested: that differences in shell thickness are inherited rather than produced by the conditions in which each snail grows.

Ecologists who later tested it raised young periwinkles from northern and southern populations in the laboratory. Some were kept in water that had flowed past green crabs fed on periwinkles; others, in crab-free water. Within a few months, the snails exposed to crab water, whichever population they came from, had built substantially thicker shells than unexposed snails from the same population, and the difference was comparable in size to the change recorded at southern sites over the past century. The thickening was not free, however. The exposed snails gained less body tissue than unexposed ones, apparently because shell added inside takes up room the body would otherwise fill. A snail that builds armor where no crabs hunt thus pays for protection it does not need, which is why a defense switched on only when predators are present can be favored over one that is always on.

The plasticity account has changed what the historical record can be taken to show: a thickening that follows a predator’s arrival is no longer, by itself, evidence that a population has evolved. Some proponents go further, holding that the southern snails of the late twentieth century differed from their nineteenth-century predecessors only in the conditions under which they grew, not in anything they inherited—though the experiments cannot show this, since they do not rule out a part for selection. Questions also remain. Cues in the laboratory may have been stronger than those snails meet on the shore, and because the southern gulf is warmer, and shell is cheaper to deposit in warm water, temperature may contribute to the north–south difference independently of crabs.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Cunningham and Cage composed dance and music separately because each believed that an artist should be free to work without adjusting to a collaborator’s choices.
By separating dance from music, Cunningham sought to give spectators the same freedom in listening that his staging gave them in deciding where to look.
Cunningham’s turn to chance procedures in the 1950s left the relation between his dances and their scores more arbitrary than it had been in the solos of the 1940s.
Cunningham’s separate composition of movement and sound with Cage reflected not indifference to how the two would relate but a different conception of their relation.

Although early reviewers judged the pairing of Cunningham’s dances with their scores to be arbitrary, the shared structures of his collaboration with Cage kept the two arts closely coordinated throughout.
questions.explanation: The passage reports the reviewers’ view that separate composition meant indifference, then shows how the method related the arts: shared time structures, and later a relation left open (“not a refusal to relate the two arts but a way of leaving their relation open”). D says this. B is the near-miss: the freedom given to listeners is one point made in the third paragraph, not the passage’s main point.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the main point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (the reviewers, then “The working method was in fact quite deliberate”); third and fourth paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: What does the passage set up and then explain? The reviewers’ idea that if dance and music were made apart, the pairing didn’t matter. Every paragraph after that shows otherwise: shared time structures (paragraph 2), a relation left open (paragraph 3), music as pressure (paragraph 4). We need an answer that says: separate making was a different kind of relation, not no relation. Most students who miss this pick (B) because it’s a real claim in the passage. But it’s one sentence of paragraph 3.

choices.note: Wrong reason. The passage never says why the two worked apart, and it never mentions a belief about artists’ freedom from collaborators.

Tempting. The passage does compare the freedom of hearing to the freedom of looking. But that is a detail in paragraph 3, offered as an extension of the main argument, and the passage doesn’t say this was Cunningham’s aim.
Opposite. The author says chance left the relation “open,” not that it made the pairing arbitrary, which was the reviewers’ word.
CORRECT. Separate composition was not indifference; it was a different way of relating the two arts. That is the thread that runs through every paragraph.
Too strong. “Closely coordinated throughout” overstates it: in the 1940s the arts met only at structural boundaries, and later even that shrank to total length.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in the solo works that Cunningham presented with Cage’s music in the mid-1940s,
choices: a framework of durations was fixed in advance, and neither artist fit the other’s work within it
each phrase of the dance was matched in advance to a corresponding phrase of the music
chance procedures determined the points at which the dance and the music would coincide
the music was composed first, and the dance was then divided to match its proportions
the dance and the music shared nothing except an agreement about each work’s total length
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the two agreed in advance on a work’s length and its division into parts and then “composed separately within it.” A restates that in other words. E is the trap: a single agreement about total length describes many later works, not the solos of the 1940s.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the passage reports about the mid-1940s solos.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Two things are true of the 1940s solos: a shared structure of time was set first (length plus parts of fixed proportions), and then each artist worked separately inside it. The right answer needs both halves. Watch out for answers that describe the later works or the conventional method.

choices.note: CORRECT. “A framework of durations” is the agreed length and proportions; “neither artist fit the other’s work within it” is “composed separately within it.”
This is the conventional method the passage says Cunningham abandoned. They coincided only at boundaries between parts, not phrase by phrase.
Wrong period. Chance procedures came in the early 1950s, and in the solos the coincidences came from the agreed structure, not chance.
Neither was composed first and fitted to the other. The structure was agreed by both before either composed.
Tempting, but wrong period. The single agreement about total length is what the structure “shrank to” in many later works. The 1940s solos also shared the division into parts.

questions.stem: By saying that the music acts on the dance “not as a guide but as a pressure” (last sentence of the passage), the author most probably means that the music
choices: sets the tempo of the dancers’ movements more forcefully than a conventional score would
creates a tension in the audience that the dance is then designed to resolve
limits the choreographic choices that Cunningham would otherwise have left to chance
guides the spectators’ attention away from the dancers and toward the sound
becomes visible chiefly in the dancers’ effort not to be swayed by it
questions.explanation: The preceding sentence says dancers must keep their phrase’s timing while unrelated sound fills the theater, and the last sentence adds that the steadiness resisting the music becomes part of what the audience sees. E captures that: the music matters through the dancers’ resistance to it. A takes “pressure” in its everyday sense of force that drives the tempo, which is the “guide” role the author denies.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret “not as a guide but as a pressure.”

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: A guide is something you follow. A pressure is something you push against. The paragraph says the dancers hold their own timing against sound that doesn’t accompany them, and that this steadiness is visible. So the music matters because of the resistance it provokes. Most students who miss this take “pressure” as “stronger control” (A). But stronger control is just a more forceful guide, which is what the author says the music is not.

choices.note: Tempting, because “pressure” sounds like force. But setting the tempo is exactly being a guide. The dancers keep their own timing.
Nothing about the music being composed to create tension or the dance resolving it. The music and dance were made separately.
Chance and choreographic choices aren’t what this sentence is about; the music arrives after the dance is made.
Borrows the word “guide” and turns it toward the audience. The passage doesn’t say the music pulls attention away from the dancers.
CORRECT. The music shapes what the audience sees by provoking a visible steadiness: the dancers’ effort to hold their timing against it.

questions.stem: The author mentions Cage’s view about duration (last sentence of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that the dance and the music in the solos of the mid-1940s were meant to coincide at every moment, not only at the boundaries between parts
show that the structures used in the collaboration were derived from Cage’s musical theories rather than from Cunningham’s choreographic ones
suggest that silence could serve as accompaniment for Cunningham’s dances as well as sound could
indicate why Cage, rather than Cunningham, determined the length of each work and the proportions of its parts
account for the suitability of a particular kind of framework as common ground for two arts that were otherwise made apart
questions.explanation: The paragraph has just described the shared time structure; Cage’s view that duration is what sound and silence have in common explains why a structure made of durations could be shared by movement too. E says this abstractly. C is the trap: it borrows “silence” from the sentence (and from the dancers learning in silence in the last paragraph), but the point is about what a structure can share, not about silence as accompaniment.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings in Cage’s view about duration.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, especially its last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Why would a passage about dance quote a composer’s theory about silence? Look at what comes right before: dance and music agreed on a structure of time and then went their own ways. Cage’s idea explains why time works as the shared ground: duration belongs to sound and silence alike, so it can belong to movement too. We want an answer about why that kind of framework could be common to both arts. Most students who miss this pick (C) because it reuses “silence.”

choices.note: Contradicts the passage. Dance and music coincided only at the boundaries between parts.
Over-reads one detail. The theory is Cage’s, but the author never says the collaboration’s structures came from Cage rather than from Cunningham, and that isn’t the point of the sentence.

Tempting, because the sentence talks about silence and the last paragraph mentions dancers learning in silence. But the sentence isn’t about using silence as accompaniment; it’s about why duration can be shared.
Wrong party. The passage says “the two agreed in advance” on the structure.
CORRECT. Cage’s view explains why a framework built of durations could be shared by two arts that were otherwise composed separately.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the relationship between the dance and the music in the solo works that Cunningham presented with Cage’s music in the mid-1940s, as the passage describes that relationship?
choices: A poet and a printmaker agree only on the total number of pages in their joint book; each then works alone, and which poem faces which print is decided by drawing lots.
A poet and a printmaker divide their joint book into twelve sections of agreed lengths; the poet completes the texts first, and the printmaker then designs each print to answer its poem.
A poet and a printmaker agree that their joint book will consist of twelve sections of specified lengths; each then supplies material for every section without seeing the other’s work.
A poet and a printmaker agree on nothing in advance; each revises the joint book page by page in response to what the other has most recently added.
A printmaker illustrates a poet’s finished book, choosing for each poem an image that matches its mood and placing it so that it begins where the poem does.
questions.explanation: The 1940s solos had two features: a structure of length and proportioned parts agreed in advance, and separate composition within it. C has both. A is the main trap: it matches the later works (a single agreement about total length plus chance), not the 1940s solos. B shares the structure but has one artist fit the other.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the 1940s relationship to a new case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (the solos); third paragraph (the later works, for contrast).

breakdown.analysis: List the elements first: 1. an agreed structure (overall length AND parts of fixed proportions); 2. each artist works within it separately; 3. no fitting of one to the other. Now check each answer against all three. The answers differ by one element, so be strict. Most students who miss this pick (A) or (B): A is the later works, and B drops element 3.

choices.note: Tempting, but this is the later works: only total length is agreed, and chance does the rest. The 1940s solos also fixed the parts.
Tempting. It has the agreed sections, but then the printmaker fits each print to its poem. That’s the conventional choreography-to-music model the passage says Cunningham abandoned.
CORRECT. Agreed sections of fixed length (structure of time) plus each artist working alone within every section (separate composition). Both elements match.
Nothing agreed in advance and constant mutual adjustment: the opposite of both elements.
One art made to fit the other, with no shared framework agreed in advance. This is the conventional model.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: The early reviewers were right that the pairing of a particular dance with a particular score was arbitrary, though wrong to conclude that the pairing did not matter.
That the dancers often first heard a score shortly before a premiere does not show that the score had little bearing on what audiences saw.
The coincidences between sound and movement in Cunningham’s later works were planned in advance, although audiences took them for accidents.
The relation between dance and music in Cunningham’s later works was less fixed than in the solos of the 1940s, and for that reason less significant to the audience’s experience.
Cunningham’s dances would have affected audiences in much the same way had they been performed without any music.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says dancers often heard the score only at or shortly before the first performance; the last paragraph says the music still matters, acting as a pressure whose resistance the audience sees. Together these support B. D is the near-miss: the later relation was indeed less fixed, but the author treats that openness as meaningful, not as a loss of significance.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author would endorse.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph (dancers heard the score late); third and fourth paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so test each answer against the author’s whole line: separation is a relation, not indifference, and the music matters even though the dance wasn’t made to it. Watch for answers that are half right. Most students who miss this pick (D), because the first half is true. The second half isn’t: the author says the openness gives spectators a freedom and makes each coincidence belong to one performance.

choices.note: The passage presents the “arbitrary” reading as the reviewers’ and answers it: in the 1940s works “the working method was in fact quite deliberate,” with a shared structure agreed in advance. So the pairing wasn’t arbitrary.

CORRECT. Paragraph 1 gives the late hearing; paragraph 4 says the music nonetheless shapes what the audience sees through the dancers’ resistance. So the late hearing doesn’t show the score was irrelevant.
Contradicts paragraph 3: because neither art was made to fit the other, coincidences belonged to one performance alone. They weren’t planned.
Half right. “Less fixed” is true of the later works. “Less significant” isn’t supported: the author presents the open relation as giving the audience a freedom.
Contradicts the last paragraph, which says the score “bore on what audiences saw” through the steadiness the dancers keep against it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The town’s stamp scrip did little to revive its retail trade, because merchants returned most certificates to the treasury instead of spending them.
Kenning’s study shows that the design of a currency can matter more to a local recovery than the quantity of money in circulation does.
Kenning’s evidence does not establish that the cost of holding the scrip, as opposed to other circumstances, brought about the town’s commercial recovery.
The reopening of local employers, rather than any feature of the scrip, explains the recovery of retail sales in Kenning’s town and in its neighbor alike.
Although Kenning’s reconstruction of the scrip’s movements is ingenious, she fails to make clear whether the town’s revival consisted in more transactions or greater sales.
questions.explanation: After crediting Kenning’s approach (and allowing that the stamps “may well have quickened trade”), the author raises three problems with her evidence: an unclear measure of revival, an assumption about merchants, and a comparison she cannot dismiss without discounting her own town. C states that. E is half the story: it is only the second paragraph’s objection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the main point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (“What her evidence shows is less clear”); the three objections; the last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: What is the author’s verdict on Kenning? Not “the stamps did nothing”: the author grants that they “may well have quickened trade.” The verdict is that Kenning hasn’t shown the stamps, rather than something else, caused the recovery. Most students who miss this pick (E), which is a real complaint but only one of three.

choices.note: Too strong. The author questions Kenning’s evidence, not the stamps’ effect, and even grants that they “may well have quickened trade.” Nor does the author say merchants failed to spend scrip “instead” of returning it; the tax returns raise a doubt, not a verdict.
This is Kenning’s implied thesis, which the author says she hasn’t established.
CORRECT. The cost of holding the scrip is the weekly stamp; “as opposed to other circumstances” covers the mill and the tax-payment use. The author’s point is that the causal claim is unproven.
Too strong. The author raises the reopening as a possible contributor, not as the explanation, and doesn’t deny the stamps had some effect.
Half right. This is the second paragraph’s objection only; the passage also attacks an assumption and an ignored comparison.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the scrip issued by the neighboring town differed from that issued by the town at the center of Kenning’s study in that the neighboring town’s scrip
choices: did not require holders to pay anything to keep it valid
was issued only after the town’s chief employer had reopened
was followed by a markedly slower recovery in retail sales
could not be redeemed for cash once a year had passed
circulated mainly among merchants rather than among residents
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the neighbor issued scrip “without any stamp requirement”; the first paragraph explains that the stamp was a weekly purchase a holder had to make to keep a certificate valid. So the neighbor’s scrip imposed no such payment: A. D is the near-miss: in Kenning’s town the stamps raised the money for redemption, but the passage says nothing about whether or how the neighbor’s scrip was redeemed. B is also tempting: the railway shop reopened in 1933 and the scrip was issued in 1933, but the passage never says which came first.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the stated difference between the two towns’ scrip.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last paragraph, first sentence; first paragraph (what the weekly stamp was).

breakdown.analysis: The neighbor’s scrip had no stamp requirement. In Kenning’s town the stamp was something a holder had to buy every week to keep the certificate valid. So the difference is that the neighbor’s holders paid nothing to keep their scrip good. The answer won’t say “stamp”; it will describe what the stamp did. Two traps go beyond the text: dates (“that year” for the railway shop and “in 1933” for the scrip don’t tell you the order) and redemption (the stamps funded it in one town, but nothing is said about the other).

choices.note: CORRECT. The stamp was a payment required to keep the certificate valid. No stamp requirement means holders paid nothing to keep it valid.
Tempting. Both events happened in 1933, but the passage doesn’t say which came first.
Opposite. The neighbor’s sales “recovered at roughly the same rate.”

Tempting, because the stamps raised the $1.04 that redeemed Kenning’s town’s certificates, so stampless scrip seems to lack that fund. But the passage never says how, or whether, the neighbor’s scrip was redeemed. That’s an inference the text doesn’t support.
Not stated. The passage describes where Kenning’s town’s scrip went, not the neighbor’s.

questions.stem: The passage provides information sufficient to answer which one of the following questions?
choices: What proportion of the certificates issued by the town at the center of Kenning’s study remained in circulation long enough to be redeemed?
Did the neighboring town begin issuing its scrip before its railway repair shop reopened?
How long after the town’s bank closed did one of its mills resume partial operation?
Had the town at the center of Kenning’s study begun issuing scrip by the time one of its mills partly reopened?
Why did the neighboring town choose to issue scrip without any stamp requirement?
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the town began issuing stamp scrip in the autumn of 1932; the last says one of its mills resumed partial operation in the summer of 1933. So the scrip came first: D is answerable. B looks parallel but isn’t: both the neighbor’s scrip and the railway shop’s reopening are dated only to 1933.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the question the passage’s facts can actually answer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph (autumn 1932); last paragraph (summer 1933; the neighbor in 1933).

breakdown.analysis: Answerable-question items punish “sounds like it’s in there.” Each wrong answer touches something the passage mentions but leaves out one fact you’d need. The right one needs you to put two dates from different paragraphs together: scrip in autumn 1932, mill in summer 1933. Most students who miss this pick (B) because it has the same shape. But for the neighbor, both events are just “1933.”

choices.note: We know “most” certificates came back within weeks, but no proportion, and nothing about redemption.
Tempting, but both events are dated only to 1933. The order is unknown.
We know when the mill reopened, but not when the bank closed (only that it was closed by autumn 1932).
CORRECT. Scrip began in the autumn of 1932; the mill resumed in the summer of 1933. Yes, the scrip came first.
The passage never gives the neighbor’s reasons.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: resolve an ambiguity in Kenning’s use of the term “revival” that the second paragraph identified
use Kenning’s own findings to suggest that the scrip may have served a purpose that required no stamps
show that the stamp records from which Kenning reconstructs the scrip’s movements are too incomplete and too scattered to support her conclusions
argue that the scrip could not have affected retail trade, since it returned to the treasury too quickly to circulate
challenge an assumption about how quickly residents spent their scrip on which Kenning’s argument depends
questions.explanation: The third paragraph uses Kenning’s own figures (certificates returned to the treasury in tax payments within weeks) to suggest the scrip may have worked mainly as a way to pay workers from future taxes, “a useful arrangement, but not one that the stamps were needed to produce.” B describes that. E is the near-miss: the paragraph does challenge an assumption, but one about merchants, not residents.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the third paragraph does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, all of it.

breakdown.analysis: Track the paragraph: Kenning assumes merchants passed scrip on as readily as residents. Her own figures say otherwise. So the scrip may have been a way to pay workers out of future taxes, which didn’t need stamps. We want an answer with the evidence (her own data) and the payoff (a stampless function). Most students who miss this pick (E) because “challenge an assumption” sounds right. Read the party: it was merchants, not residents.

choices.note: That ambiguity is raised in paragraph 2 and never resolved. Paragraph 3 moves on (“also”).
CORRECT. Her own figures on where certificates went support an alternative role for the scrip, paying workers out of future taxes, that didn’t require the stamps.
The author calls the reconstruction “ingenious” and uses its figures. Their reliability isn’t questioned.

Too strong. The author calls the arrangement “useful” and allows that the stamps “may well have quickened trade.” The paragraph questions how far the scrip circulated, not whether it could affect trade at all.
Tempting, but wrong party. The assumption challenged is that merchants passed scrip on as readily as residents did.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the second paragraph?
choices: Kenning’s figures show that the total value of the town’s retail sales did not rise while its scrip circulated.
Part of Kenning’s evidence of revival might have been produced by the very feature of the scrip she credits with the revival.
The number of transactions that the town’s merchants recorded is a less reliable figure than the total value of their sales.
Residents of the town generally broke their purchases into smaller ones in order to pass on scrip before the next stamp came due.
A charge on holding money tends to raise total spending only if it also raises the number of purchases people make.
questions.explanation: Kenning sometimes counts more transactions as revival; the author notes that residents might have split purchases “to pass on scrip before the next stamp came due.” So the stamp, the feature Kenning credits with the revival, could itself inflate one of her measures of it. That is B, stated abstractly. D is the trap: the paragraph raises splitting only as a possibility (“if”), not as what residents generally did.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the second paragraph supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph; first paragraph for what the stamp is.

breakdown.analysis: Ask what the splitting scenario does to Kenning’s argument. Why would residents break up purchases? To get rid of scrip before the next stamp came due. That’s the stamp at work. And one of her measures of revival is the count of transactions. So the stamp could raise her evidence without any real revival. The right answer won’t say “stamp” or “transactions”; it describes that loop. Most students who miss this pick (D) because it repeats the paragraph’s words. But the paragraph says “if,” and D says “generally.”

choices.note: Too strong. The author says sales could have stagnated, not that Kenning’s figures show they did.
CORRECT. The stamp (the feature she credits) could lead residents to split purchases, which raises the transaction count (one of her measures of revival) without any real increase in sales.
Reliability isn’t the issue. Both figures could be perfectly accurate; the problem is that they measure different things.
Tempting. These are the paragraph’s words, but there they are a possibility (“if residents merely broke their purchases”), not a finding.
Not supported. The paragraph says transactions could rise without total sales rising; it says nothing about what total spending requires.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author’s attitude toward the claim that the stamp requirement contributed to the town’s recovery?
choices: confident that the requirement sped up spending but doubtful that faster spending increased total sales
convinced that whatever contribution the requirement made was outweighed by the partial reopening of a mill
doubtful that any evidence could separate the requirement’s effects from those of the town’s other circumstances
persuaded that the claim would be confirmed if the revival were measured by the total value of sales
unconvinced by the case made for it, though unwilling to rule it out
questions.explanation: The author allows that the stamps “may well have quickened trade as she says,” then argues that Kenning’s evidence does not show it. E captures both halves abstractly. C is the near-miss: the author doubts that Kenning’s evidence isolates the stamps’ effect, not that any evidence could; the objections themselves point to evidence (such as the timing of the recovery relative to the mill) that would bear on the question. A gives the author a confidence that “may well” does not express.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the author’s stance on the stamps’ contribution.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, first three sentences; third and fourth paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: Two signals. The author grants that the stamps “may well have quickened trade as she says,” so the claim isn’t rejected. Then: “What her evidence shows is less clear,” followed by three objections, so the claim isn’t accepted either. Prephrase: open to it, unpersuaded by the support. Watch for answers that turn a doubt about this evidence into a doubt about all evidence (C), or that turn “may well” into confidence (A).

choices.note: Tempting, because it mixes belief and doubt. But “may well have” is not confidence, and the third paragraph even suggests the scrip mostly went straight back to the treasury.
Too strong. The mill is raised as a possible contributor, and nothing is weighed against anything.

Tempting, because the author does say other circumstances could explain the recovery. But the complaint is about Kenning’s evidence, not about evidence in principle. The author’s own objections suggest what could settle the matter (when the recovery happened relative to the mill, how far scrip circulated).
Not stated. The author points out that Kenning’s measure is unclear but never says a different measure would confirm her claim.
CORRECT. Unwilling to rule it out (“may well have quickened trade”) but unconvinced by the case (“What her evidence shows is less clear,” then three objections).

questions.stem: With which one of the following statements would the author be most likely to agree?
choices: Had the town’s scrip carried no weekly charge, its residents would probably have spent each certificate about as quickly as they actually did.
Kenning erred in relying on surviving stamp records to reconstruct how the town’s scrip moved among its holders.
Even certificates that cost nothing to hold might have provided part of the benefit the town derived from its scrip.
The partial reopening of one of the town’s mills was the chief cause of the revival of the town’s retail trade.
Kenning’s town would have recovered at the same rate as its neighbor even if it had never issued any scrip.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph suggests the scrip may have served chiefly to pay workers out of future tax receipts, “a useful arrangement, but not one that the stamps were needed to produce.” C says this with the author’s hedge. A is the strong trap: it overreaches from “the stamps weren’t needed for this function” to a prediction about spending speed that the author never makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author would endorse.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last sentence; last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: What does the author think the scrip might really have done? Paid workers out of future taxes. Did that need the stamp? No. So some of the scrip’s benefit was available without the charge. Notice the hedges you need: “might,” “at least part.” Most students who miss this pick (A), which makes a claim about spending speed the author never makes.

choices.note: Tempting, but it overreaches. The author doubts the stamps’ effect can be read from the figures; that’s not a prediction that spending speed would be unchanged.
Opposite. The author calls the reconstruction “ingenious” and treats its figures as evidence.
CORRECT. The pay-from-future-taxes function “was not one that the stamps were needed to produce,” so a stampless certificate could have provided at least that benefit.
Too strong. The mill is offered as something that could have contributed, not as the chief cause.
Too strong and not supported. The author never claims scrip did nothing for the town.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help Kenning to answer the objection concerning the neighboring town that is raised in the last paragraph?
choices: Nearly all of the rise in her town’s retail sales came before the spring of 1933.
Surviving stamp records show that residents of Kenning’s town usually spent each new certificate within a few days of receiving it.
The neighboring town’s scrip, like that of Kenning’s town, could be used to pay property taxes, and merchants there often used it that way.
Several other towns that issued scrip with a stamp requirement in the same years saw no recovery in their retail sales.
Fewer of the neighboring town’s merchants than of those in Kenning’s town agreed to accept their town’s scrip during its first year.
questions.explanation: The objection is that a reopened employer could explain the recovery in Kenning’s town as well, since one of its mills resumed partial operation in the summer of 1933. If nearly all the rise came before that summer, the mill cannot account for it, which answers the objection: A. B is the strong trap; fast spending supports Kenning’s mechanism in general but does nothing about the mill.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Help Kenning answer the specific objection in the last paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last paragraph (the neighboring town, the railway shop, the mill in the summer of 1933); first paragraph (scrip began in the autumn of 1932).

breakdown.analysis: What exactly is the objection? Kenning dismisses the neighbor because a railway shop reopened there. The author says: your town had a reopening too, a mill in the summer of 1933, so the same factor could explain your recovery. To answer that, Kenning needs to cut the mill out of her town’s story. Timing does it. Scrip began in the autumn of 1932; if the sales rise was basically finished by the spring of 1933, a summer reopening can’t have caused it. Most students pick (B) because it is strong evidence for Kenning’s mechanism. But the question asks about one objection, and fast spending is compatible with the mill driving the recovery.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the rise was nearly complete before the mill reopened in the summer of 1933, the reopening can’t explain it, so the parallel with the neighbor’s railway shop fails.
Tempting. It supports the stamps’ effect on spending speed. But it doesn’t touch the mill: residents could spend quickly and the recovery could still come from the reopening.
If anything this makes the two towns’ scrip more alike, which makes the neighbor’s stampless recovery more damaging to Kenning.
This hurts Kenning: stamps without recovery elsewhere suggests stamps aren’t enough.

About the neighbor’s scrip, not Kenning’s town. If anything it suggests the neighbor recovered without much help from scrip, but the objection is that a reopening could explain Kenning’s own town, and this says nothing about her mill.

questions.stem: According to passage A, the physicians whom Brann asked about medical errors
choices: apologized less often after medical errors than other hospital staff did
said they would apologize more readily if apology statutes were adopted
cited legal exposure less often than they cited embarrassment or institutional habit
reported that institutional habit discouraged their patients from suing the hospital
named some reasons that no evidentiary rule could address
questions.explanation: The third paragraph of passage A says the physicians cited embarrassment, uncertainty, and institutional habit “at least as often as legal exposure,” and that “A rule of evidence can do nothing about these.” E restates that abstractly. C is the near-miss: “at least as often” allows those reasons to have been cited exactly as often as legal exposure, so “less often” goes beyond the text.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says about Brann’s physicians.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The physicians gave several reasons for not apologizing: embarrassment, uncertainty, institutional habit, and legal exposure, the first three “at least as often as” the last. The author adds that a rule of evidence “can do nothing about these.” So the answer is that some of their reasons lie outside what an evidence rule can touch. Watch “at least as often”: it means equal or more, not more.

choices.note: No comparison with other staff appears.
Not stated. The study asked why they hadn’t apologized, not what a statute would change.
Tempting, but too strong. “At least as often” allows a tie. The passage doesn’t say legal exposure came up less often than the other reasons.
Garbles the detail. Institutional habit was a reason the physicians didn’t apologize, not something that affected patients’ suing.
CORRECT. Embarrassment, uncertainty, and habit are reasons that, as the author says, “a rule of evidence can do nothing about.”

questions.stem: By “ordinary evidentiary grounds” (last sentence of the first paragraph of passage B), the author of passage B most probably means
choices: the observation, drawn from everyday experience, that people often apologize for harms they did not cause
the standards jurors ordinarily use in deciding whether a defendant’s apology after an accident was sincere
the reasons that legislators usually give for laws designed to change how people behave
the reasoning by which courts weigh what a statement proves against how a jury is likely to take it
the long-standing rule that a defendant’s own admission of fault may not be offered against him
questions.explanation: The paragraph opens with the evidence-law principle of excluding statements whose persuasive power outruns their value as proof, and calls apology laws defensible on those grounds “whatever their effect on how often people apologize.” D paraphrases that weighing. A is the near-miss: it is the illustration the paragraph uses, not the grounds themselves.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret “ordinary evidentiary grounds” in passage B.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The “grounds” are the principle in the first sentence: keep out statements whose power to persuade a jury outruns their value as proof. “Ordinary” means this is the usual business of evidence law, not something special to apologies. And “whatever their effect on how often people apologize” tells you these grounds aren’t about encouraging apologies. Most students who miss this pick (A), which is the example used to show the principle applies, not the principle.

choices.note: Tempting. It’s the observation that shows sympathy proves little. But the grounds are the weighing principle that observation feeds into.
Jurors don’t set standards here; the passage says jurors misread apologies, which is the problem the grounds address.
Opposite direction. The grounds are explicitly independent of changing behavior (“whatever their effect on how often people apologize”).
CORRECT. Weighing a statement’s value as proof against its power to persuade a jury is the standard evidentiary reasoning the paragraph invokes.
Not the passage’s point, and not a real rule: passage A notes that admissions of fault are “fully admissible.”

questions.stem: In the second paragraph of passage B, the author’s acknowledgment that fear of litigation “may be only one of several reasons” people withhold apologies serves primarily to
choices: concede a point to critics without accepting what they infer from it
concede that laws protecting apologies are unlikely to change how often people apologize
explain why the evidentiary case for such laws does not depend on their effect on how often people apologize
suggest that such laws should be supplemented by measures addressing people’s other reasons for withholding apologies
introduce evidence that legal exposure is the most important reason people fail to apologize
questions.explanation: The author allows that fear of litigation may be only one reason, then argues that removing one deterrent still leaves fewer, so the laws’ effect “is likely to be real.” A describes that concede-then-deny move abstractly. C is the trap: it repeats the first paragraph’s point, but this sentence defends the laws’ effect on apologies rather than setting it aside.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the “only one of several reasons” remark does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph; compare passage A, third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Look at the shape of the sentence: “X may be true, but Y.” X is a premise a skeptic would use (people withhold apologies for many reasons, so a rule of evidence won’t help). Y says the laws still help. So the author grants the premise and rejects the doubt. Most students who miss this pick (C) because the first paragraph did set the effect aside. This paragraph comes back to the effect and defends it.

choices.note: CORRECT. The author grants a point a critic would use (many reasons besides fear) and denies the critic’s inference (the laws won’t help), since removing one deterrent still helps.
Opposite. The paragraph opens “That effect is likely to be real.”
Tempting, but that’s the job of the first paragraph’s “whatever their effect.” This sentence argues that the effect is real.
Not said. “A law need not cure a problem to be worth having” defends the law as it is; no other measures are proposed.
Opposite. The remark concedes that legal exposure may be only one of several reasons.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately characterizes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A raises several objections to a type of law; passage B answers each of those objections in turn.
Passage A argues that a type of law has failed to achieve its goals; passage B argues that those goals were misconceived.
Passage A questions the assumptions usually offered in support of a type of law; passage B defends such laws partly on a ground independent of those assumptions.
Passage A objects to a type of law; passage B grants those objections but holds that the law’s benefit to the accuracy of jury verdicts outweighs all of them.
Passage A and passage B offer competing explanations of why people who have caused an injury are often reluctant to apologize for it.
questions.explanation: Passage A says apology statutes “rest on uncertain ground,” challenging the rationale that they encourage apologies and discourage suits. Passage B defends the laws first on evidentiary grounds that hold “whatever their effect on how often people apologize,” then disputes some of A’s doubts. C fits. A is the near-miss: B never addresses A’s worry about strategic use, so it does not answer each objection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the passages relate.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, first paragraph (the rationale and “uncertain ground”); passage B, first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: What does A attack? The rationale: statutes encourage apologies, and apologies reduce suits. What does B do? Leads with a reason for the laws that doesn’t depend on that rationale at all (excluding misleading evidence), then pushes back on some of A’s doubts. Most students who miss this pick (A), which describes the tidy point-by-point rebuttal they expect. But B never touches A’s strongest worry, strategic use by insurers.

choices.note: Tempting, but B doesn’t answer each objection. It never addresses A’s worry about insurers using the statutes strategically.
A doesn’t say the laws have failed, and B doesn’t call the goals misconceived; B thinks the laws do encourage apologies.
CORRECT. A questions the assumptions behind the usual rationale; B’s evidentiary argument holds regardless of those assumptions, and B also disputes some of A’s doubts (hence “partly”).
B doesn’t grant A’s objections; it disputes the claim that the laws do little and that sympathy-only apologies are empty.
Only A discusses reasons for not apologizing in any detail, and B concedes there may be several. They don’t offer competing explanations.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the use of apology statutes that the author of passage A calls “most troubling” (last paragraph of passage A)?
choices: A hospital instructs its physicians to admit their errors candidly to injured patients, in the hope that such candor will make the patients less inclined to sue.
A city shields bystanders from liability when they give aid at accident scenes, and as a result more bystanders begin offering aid.
A landlord whose neglected stairway injured several tenants has his manager express warm regret, which the law keeps from juries, so that the tenants will not consult lawyers.
An airline offers stranded passengers heartfelt apologies, which a regulation bars from use in court, and few of the passengers, most of whose claims are weak, go on to sue.
A company that had planned to apologize to customers injured by its product decides against doing so after its lawyers warn that any apology could later be used against it in court.
questions.explanation: The troubling use has three parts: regret that costs nothing legally, offered deliberately, to defuse claims that deserve to be pursued. C has all three: protected statements, offered to keep tenants from lawyers, about an injury the landlord caused by neglect. D is the near-miss: protected apologies and fewer suits, but the claims are mostly weak, so nothing deserving is defused. A uses apologies to reduce suits, but admissions of fault are not legally weightless.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match passage A’s “most troubling” use to a new case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: List the elements: 1. regret with no legal weight (protected by the statute); 2. offered strategically; 3. to defuse claims that deserve to be pursued. Check all three. Most students who miss this pick (D), which has elements 1 and 2 but fails 3: the claims are mostly weak, so defusing them isn’t the injustice A worries about. Or (A), which is strategic but not weightless: admissions of fault are fully admissible.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s a strategic apology to reduce suits. But admissions of fault aren’t protected, so they aren’t legally weightless, and candor about fault is the kind of apology A wants.
This is the statutes’ intended effect in another setting, not their abuse.
CORRECT. Protected regret (element 1), offered deliberately to keep tenants from lawyers (element 2), for injuries caused by the landlord’s neglect, which are claims worth pursuing (element 3).
Tempting, but the claims are mostly weak, so the apologies aren’t defusing claims that deserve to be pursued.
This is the problem the statutes were meant to solve (fear of litigation), not their strategic misuse.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: a protected expression of sympathy falls short of what at least some injured people want from those who have harmed them
fear of litigation is one of the reasons that people withhold apologies after causing harm
laws protecting expressions of sympathy lead people to offer more apologies than they otherwise would
jurors tend to interpret a defendant’s expression of sympathy as an admission of fault
acknowledging an injury without accepting blame gives many injured people what they most want
questions.explanation: Passage A says sympathy-only apologies are the kind injured people “find least satisfying” and give them “little or nothing of what they seek.” Passage B says that for many injured people “what matters first is that the harm be acknowledged.” That is a disagreement: E. C is the dominant trap: B says the laws’ effect on apologies is real, but A never denies they produce more apologies; its last paragraph worries about the strategic apologies they encourage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a point the two authors take opposite sides on.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second and fourth paragraphs; passage B, second and third paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one author must say yes and the other no. A: sympathy without fault gives injured people little or nothing of what they seek. B: for many, acknowledgment is what matters first. That’s a clean yes/no on whether such an apology meets what many injured people most want. Most students who miss this pick (C), because A sounds skeptical of the laws. But A never says they won’t produce more apologies. A’s worry about insurers coaching policyholders assumes they will.

choices.note: Both agree. A says such apologies sidestep responsibility; B grants that “some injured people want” a confession of fault.
Both agree. A’s physicians cite legal exposure among other reasons, and B concedes fear is “only one of several reasons.”
Tempting, because B affirms it and A sounds doubtful. But A only says other deterrents remain, and its strategic-use paragraph assumes the statutes do bring forth more (weightless) apologies.
Only B addresses jurors. A says nothing either way.
CORRECT. A: sympathy without fault gives “little or nothing of what they seek.” B: for many, acknowledgment of the harm “matters first.”

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a criticism that the author of passage A would be most likely to offer regarding the studies of settlement negotiations mentioned in passage B?
choices: Because sympathy that admits no fault gives injured people little of what they seek, the claimants’ greater receptiveness to offers must have had some other cause.
Their findings are what one would expect if regret led injured people to press claims less than their injuries warranted.
They do not show that fear of litigation, rather than embarrassment or institutional habit, is what keeps people from apologizing after causing harm.
Claimants already negotiating settlements are unlike most injured people, most of whom never press claims.
They show only that expressions of sympathy make claimants more receptive to offers, not that they make claimants less likely to consult a lawyer.
questions.explanation: Passage B reads the finding that sympathy makes some claimants more receptive to settlement offers as a sign that acknowledgment gives them what they want. Passage A’s last paragraph warns that soothing words can lead people to drop claims that deserve to be pursued, so A would say the finding fits its own worry just as well: B. A is the dominant trap: it uses A’s own words, but A grants that soothing works (a soothed person is “less likely to consult a lawyer”), so A would not deny that the sympathy made claimants more receptive.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the criticism passage A’s author would make of the settlement studies.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, third paragraph (the study); passage A, second and fourth paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: What does B take the studies to show? That acknowledgment satisfies people, since it makes them more receptive to offers. Would A deny the sympathy made them settle? No. A’s whole “most troubling” point is that soothing words make people back off. So A’s criticism is that settling more readily isn’t proof of satisfaction; it’s exactly what you’d see if people were being talked out of claims worth pursuing. Most students who miss this pick (A), because it quotes passage A. It fails because A concedes that soothing works. A’s objection is to what that soothing does to people’s claims.

choices.note: Tempting, because it echoes A’s second paragraph. But A’s fourth paragraph grants that soothing words make people less likely to pursue claims, so A wouldn’t say the sympathy couldn’t have caused the settlements.
CORRECT. A’s strategic-use worry predicts exactly this result: regret leads people to accept less than their claims deserve. So the finding doesn’t show the apologies gave claimants what they wanted.
Uses A’s Brann point, but the studies aren’t about why people withhold apologies, so this criticism misses its target.
A generic sampling complaint that A never raises. Nothing in A turns on who negotiates settlements.
A wouldn’t press this. A holds that soothed people are less likely to consult lawyers, and greater receptiveness to offers fits that worry rather than counting against it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The thicker shells of southern flat periwinkles show that natural selection by green crabs can transform a snail population within a few decades.
Laboratory experiments have shown that the thickening of periwinkle shells in the Gulf of Maine was a response to crab cues rather than the product of natural selection.
Water temperature, rather than the presence of green crabs, accounts for most of the north–south difference in the thickness of flat periwinkle shells.
Evidence that periwinkles can thicken their shells in response to predators has undercut, without wholly settling, the evolutionary reading of the gulf’s shell record.
Because thick shells are costly to build, periwinkles in the northern gulf, where crabs arrived late, have been slower than southern ones to evolve heavy armor.
questions.explanation: The passage presents the evolutionary explanation, the experiments showing crab-induced thickening, the conclusion that a post-predator thickening is no longer by itself evidence of evolution, and the questions that remain. D says this with the author’s reservation. B is the near-miss: it overstates, since the author says the experiments do not rule out a part for selection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the main point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second through fourth paragraphs, especially the last.

breakdown.analysis: The passage moves: evolutionary explanation → its untested assumption → experiments showing the thickening can be induced → the record no longer proves evolution on its own → questions that remain. The right answer keeps the reservation. Most students who miss this pick (B), which drops it: the author says the experiments can’t rule out a part for selection.

choices.note: This is the first explanation, which the passage says rested on an untested assumption.
Tempting, but too strong. The author says the experiments “do not rule out a part for selection.”
Temperature is raised as a possible contributor, not the main cause.

CORRECT. Inducible thickening undercuts reading the shell record as evolution (“no longer, by itself, evidence”), while the caveats about selection, cue strength, and temperature supply the “without wholly settling.”
Treats the evolutionary story as settled and adds a claim (slower evolution in the north) the passage never makes.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that if young flat periwinkles drifted as larvae instead of crawling away from where they hatched, then
choices: the snails would have been less able, as individuals, to thicken their shells in response to waterborne cues from crabs
differences in shell thickness between northern and southern snails could not have arisen
green crabs would have reached the northern part of the gulf sooner than they did
northern populations would have encountered green crabs as early as southern populations did
the evolutionary explanation would fit less well with how quickly the shells had changed
questions.explanation: The second paragraph cites the crawling young as the reason crab-exposed populations “could have diverged genetically from others within relatively few generations.” Drifting larvae would mix populations, making quick divergence harder to credit, so the evolutionary story would fit the decades-long timescale less well: E. B is the dominant trap: it forgets the third paragraph, where crab cues produce thickness differences with no genetic divergence at all.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what follows if the young drifted.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, second sentence; third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Why does the passage mention crawling young? Because they stay near home, so a crab-exposed population doesn’t mix much with others and can diverge in a few generations. If the young drifted, populations would mix, and fast genetic divergence becomes harder to believe. That hurts the evolutionary story’s claim to explain change “within decades.” Most students who miss this pick (B). But the plasticity findings show thickness differences can arise without any genetic divergence, so drifting larvae wouldn’t rule them out.

choices.note: Mixes up the two accounts. Crawling young matter for genetic divergence; the ability to thicken in response to cues has nothing to do with how the young disperse.
Tempting, but too strong. The plasticity experiments show differences can arise from growing conditions alone, which drifting larvae wouldn’t prevent.
How snails disperse doesn’t affect how fast crabs spread.
Confuses snails’ movement with crabs’. The order of exposure depends on the crab’s spread.
CORRECT. Crawling young are what made divergence “within relatively few generations” plausible. Without them, the evolutionary account fits a change of decades less well.

questions.stem: The author’s statement that the exposed snails gained less body tissue than unexposed ones (third paragraph) functions primarily to
choices: help account for the defense’s being deployed only as needed
identify a limitation of the laboratory experiments to which the author returns in the final paragraph
