suggest that the thickening observed in the laboratory was a symptom of stress rather than a defense against crabs
show that thickened shells protect periwinkles from green crabs less well than had been assumed
provide evidence that the difference in shell thickness between northern and southern snails is inherited
questions.explanation: Less tissue shows that thickening has a cost; that cost is why a defense switched on only when predators are present can be favored over one that is always on. A states this in other words. C is the trap: slower growth can look like a sign of stress, but the passage explains it by the space the added shell takes up and treats the thickening as protection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author mentions the tissue result.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence comes right after “The thickening was not free.” So it establishes a cost. What is the cost used for? To explain why it pays to build armor only when crabs are around. The right answer will describe that without saying “switched on.” Most students who miss this pick (C), because less growth sounds unhealthy. But the passage attributes it to room taken up by shell and calls the shell “armor.”

choices.note: CORRECT. The cost explains why thickening only when crabs are present can be favored over always having thick shells: a defense used only as needed avoids paying for unneeded armor.
The final paragraph’s caveats are about cue strength, temperature, and selection, not tissue growth.
Tempting, because reduced growth can signal stress. But the passage explains the reduced tissue by the room the added shell takes up, and calls the thickening “armor” and “protection.”
Nothing about how well thick shells protect; the passage assumes they protect.
Opposite. The experiment is part of the case that thickness can be induced rather than inherited.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the change in shell thickness recorded at southern sites between the late nineteenth century and the late twentieth?
choices: It reflects differences in the conditions under which the earlier and later snails grew rather than any change in what the snails inherited.
It was larger than any change in shell thickness that crab cues could have produced without some change in the snails’ inherited makeup.
It was produced at least in part by the warmer water of the southern part of the gulf.
It roughly equals a change that snails were induced to make within months, perhaps by cues stronger than those on the shore.
It occurred too quickly to have resulted from natural selection acting on the southern population.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says crab water produced, within months, thickening comparable to the change recorded at southern sites over the past century; the fourth paragraph cautions that laboratory cues may have been stronger than those on the shore. D combines the two. A is the dominant trap: it is the view of the proponents who “go further,” which the author says the experiments cannot show.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s view of the southern sites’ historical change.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph (the two collections); third paragraph (“comparable in size”); fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Combine the facts: the lab thickening was comparable to the century-long southern change, and it happened in months. But the author adds a caveat: lab cues may be stronger than shore cues. So the author would say the change is matched by an induced change, with a qualifier about lab conditions. Most students who miss this pick (A), which sounds like the passage’s thesis. It’s the proponents’ stronger claim, and the author says the experiments can’t show it.

choices.note: Tempting, but this is the claim of the proponents who “go further.” The author says the experiments cannot show it, since selection may also have played a part.
Contradicts the third paragraph: crab cues alone produced a change of comparable size.
Temperature is raised only for the north–south difference, not for change over time at southern sites.
CORRECT. The lab thickening, produced within months, was comparable in size to the century’s change; the author’s caveat that lab cues may have been stronger supplies the qualifier.
Contradicts the second paragraph, which says divergence “within relatively few generations” was possible.

questions.stem: Which one of the following experiments would be most useful in determining whether water temperature contributes to the north–south difference in shell thickness independently of crabs, as the last paragraph suggests it may?
choices: raising young snails from northern and southern populations in water free of crab cues, each at the temperature typical of its home sites, and comparing their shells
raising young snails from a single population at northern and southern temperatures, all in water that has flowed past crabs, and comparing their shells
comparing the shells of wild snails at northern and southern sites where green crabs are now about equally abundant
raising young snails of one population in crab-free water, some at northern temperatures and some at southern ones, and comparing their shells
comparing the dates at which green crabs first reached northern and southern sites with the water temperatures recorded at those sites
questions.explanation: To test temperature’s effect apart from crabs, vary temperature, remove crab cues, and hold population constant so inherited differences can’t interfere. D does all three. A is the dominant trap: it removes crabs, but it pairs each population with its own temperature, so any difference could be inherited. B varies temperature but keeps crab cues, so it can’t show an effect independent of them.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the experiment that isolates temperature’s effect, apart from crabs.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, second sentence; third paragraph (the design of the crab experiments).

breakdown.analysis: Three things must be controlled: crabs (absent), population (the same), temperature (varied). Check each answer for all three. Most students who miss this pick (A), because it removes crabs and varies temperature. But it varies population along with temperature, so a difference could just be inheritance. (B) varies temperature cleanly but leaves crab cues in, so any effect might be temperature amplifying the crab response.

choices.note: Tempting, but population and temperature change together. Thicker southern shells could be inherited rather than caused by warmth.
Tempting. Temperature is isolated from population, but crab cues are present, so you can’t tell whether warmth works on its own or only strengthens the response to crabs.
Wild snails differ in population and in many site conditions besides temperature.
CORRECT. One population (inheritance held constant), no crab cues (crabs removed), two temperatures (the variable of interest).
Says nothing about shells. It looks only at crab arrival and temperature.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the position of the proponents who, according to the last paragraph, “go further”?
choices: Water at southern sites in the gulf has grown steadily warmer over the past century, and periwinkles of every population deposit shell more readily in warmer water.
Late-twentieth-century southern snails, raised without crab cues in water as cool as the gulf was a century earlier, build thicker shells than nineteenth-century southern snails had.
Periwinkles with thick shells survive attacks by green crabs considerably more often than do periwinkles of the same size with thin shells.
In the laboratory, southern snails exposed to crab cues thickened their shells by no more than northern snails that were exposed to the same cues.
In several other snail species, populations newly exposed to crabs have evolved measurably thicker shells within only a few decades.
questions.explanation: The proponents hold that the later southern snails differed from the earlier ones only in their growing conditions, not in what they inherited. If later snails, with crab cues removed and temperature set back to the earlier level, still build thicker shells than the nineteenth-century ones, the difference is not explained by those conditions and is likely inherited: B. A is the dominant trap: it offers a rival to crabs, but warmer water is another growing condition, so it supports the proponents.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Undermine the claim that the two southern collections differed only in growing conditions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, the sentence about proponents who “go further”; first paragraph (the two collections).

breakdown.analysis: Pin down the claim: the difference is conditions, not inheritance. Not “crabs, not temperature.” To undermine it, remove the conditions and see whether the difference survives. Take crab cues away, set the water back to old temperatures; if modern-stock snails are still thicker than the old ones, something inherited changed. Most students who miss this pick (A), because a rival cause usually weakens. Here the rival is another growing condition, so it supports the proponents.

choices.note: Tempting, but warmer water is a growing condition. If anything it supports the claim that the snails differed only in their conditions.
CORRECT. With crabs and warmth both removed, the later stock still builds thicker shells than the nineteenth-century snails, so the difference isn’t just conditions. Something inherited changed.
Shows crabs could select for thick shells, but not that they did. Both sides accept that thick shells protect.
Fits the proponents: equal responsiveness suggests no inherited change in the capacity to respond.
Other species show only that fast evolution is possible, which the passage already grants. It says nothing about these periwinkles.

questions.stimulus: Film critic: Many viewers assume that a remake exists only to cash in on the reputation of the original film. Some remakes surely do. But the new remake of the thriller Glass Harbor deserves to be watched on its own merits. Its director moved the story from a crowded city to a remote fishing village, and that change gives the familiar plot a sense of isolation the original never had. Admittedly, the remake’s dialogue is weaker than the original’s.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the film critic’s argument?
choices: Many remakes exist only to cash in on the reputation of the original film.
The remake of Glass Harbor has weaker dialogue than the original film has.
The remake of Glass Harbor is worth watching for its own qualities.
Moving a story to a new setting can give a familiar plot qualities the original lacked.
The remake of Glass Harbor is a better film than the original Glass Harbor.
questions.explanation: The critic grants that some remakes are cash-ins and that this one’s dialogue is weaker, but argues that the new setting makes the Glass Harbor remake worth watching on its own merits, which C restates. E is tempting, but the critic never ranks the remake above the original; a film can be worth watching without being better.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new Glass Harbor remake deserves to be watched on its own merits.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Its new fishing-village setting gives the plot an isolation the original lacked (support); some remakes are cash-ins and its dialogue is weaker (concessions).

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first sentence is a popular view, and ‘Some remakes surely do’ is a concession to it. ‘But’ flips to the critic’s own view: this remake is worth watching for itself. The setting change is the reason given for that. The ‘Admittedly’ sentence is another concession. We need an answer that says the remake deserves to be watched on its own merits.

choices.note: This is the popular view the critic pushes back on. The critic even grants that some remakes are like this, but that’s a concession, not the point.
This is the ‘Admittedly’ concession. Concessions are things the author grants despite the conclusion, not the conclusion itself.

CORRECT. ‘Worth watching for its own qualities’ is just a restatement of ‘deserves to be watched on its own merits.’ The setting change supports it; the other sentences are background and concessions.
Too general, and it’s a premise. The critic says this particular setting change helped this particular film. That supports the conclusion; it isn’t the conclusion.

Tempting. It sounds like a fan’s verdict. But the critic never compares the films overall, and even admits the dialogue is worse. ‘Worth watching’ isn’t ‘better than the original.’ Watch for unsupported rankings.

questions.stimulus:
Ilse: The town council should drop its rule that every new house include two off-street parking spaces. The rule adds thousands of dollars to the price of each new house, and many buyers own just one car.

Marco: Dropping the rule would push hundreds more cars onto our narrow streets, which already leave snowplows barely enough room each winter. Keeping new houses affordable matters, but not that much.
questions.stem: Ilse and Marco disagree over whether
choices: the parking rule makes new houses in the town more expensive than they would otherwise be
the town would be better off if new houses were no longer required to include off-street parking
many of the people who buy new houses in the town own only a single car
snowplows would be unable to clear the town’s streets if more cars were parked on them
keeping new houses affordable is a goal that the town council ought to take seriously
questions.explanation: Ilse says the parking requirement should go; Marco says dropping it would clog the streets and that affordability isn’t worth that, so he wants it kept. (B) restates that dispute in new words. (E) is the trap: Marco says affordability ‘matters,’ so on that they agree; they differ only on whether it outweighs the street problem.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ilse: drop the two-space rule, because it raises prices and many buyers have one car; Marco: dropping it would jam the narrow streets, and affordability isn’t worth that.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Ilse’s position is plain: get rid of the rule. Marco never says ‘keep the rule’ in those words, but he argues that dropping it would be bad and that cheaper houses aren’t worth that cost. So the real fight is whether the town is better off without the requirement. Watch out for the things they quietly agree on: Marco never denies the rule raises prices, and he says affordability matters.

choices.note: Both accept this. Ilse says it outright, and Marco’s ‘keeping new houses affordable matters, but not that much’ concedes that the rule costs buyers money.
CORRECT. Ilse: yes, drop the requirement. Marco: no, dropping it would push cars onto streets the plows can barely clear. That’s the point at issue, stated in different words from the stimulus.
Only Ilse speaks to this. Marco never says anything about how many cars buyers own.
Too strong, and only Marco is in the neighborhood. He says the plows ‘barely’ have room now, not that they’d be unable to clear the streets. Ilse says nothing about plows.
Tempting, because affordability is Ilse’s main reason. But Marco agrees it ‘matters.’ They disagree about how much it should weigh against the streets, not about whether it counts.

questions.stimulus: To save money, a city’s recreation department plans to end the evening van service that takes older residents home after classes at the community center. But many of the older residents who attend these evening classes now rely on the van to get home. So ending the van service will reduce attendance at the center’s evening classes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: The van service costs the recreation department more each year than any of its other programs for older residents does.
At least some of the residents who now rely on the van would not find another way to get home from the evening classes.
The money saved by ending the van service will be enough to justify a modest decline in attendance at the evening classes.
Most of the people who attend the community center’s evening classes are older residents rather than younger adults.
The recreation department could not save as much money by ending some other program that serves the city’s older residents.
questions.explanation: Relying on the van now doesn’t mean being stranded without it; riders might switch to taxis, family or neighbors. The argument needs at least some of them not to find another way home, which is (B). (C) is tempting because it sounds like the department’s reasoning, but the argument only predicts lower attendance; it never claims the savings are worth it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ending the van service will reduce evening-class attendance.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Many older attendees now rely on the van to get home.

breakdown.analysis: So what if they rely on the van now? People who rely on something can often replace it once it’s gone. If every rider simply found another ride, attendance wouldn’t budge. We need an answer that says at least some riders won’t replace the van. Use the negation test: an assumption is required if negating it wrecks the argument.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The cost of the van compared with other programs bears on whether cutting it is wise, not on whether attendance will drop. Negate it and nothing changes.
choices.negation: The van service does not cost more than every other program for older residents.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: every van rider would find another way home. Then nobody has to stop coming, and the predicted drop in attendance has no support. The argument needs this.
choices.negation: Every resident who now relies on the van would find another way to get home from the evening classes.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the department’s side of the story. But the argument only predicts that attendance will fall; it doesn’t say the cut is worth it. Negate it: the savings don’t justify the drop. The prediction is untouched.
choices.negation: The money saved by ending the van service will not be enough to justify a modest decline in attendance.

choices.note: Too strong and beside the point. The argument needs older riders to make up some of the attendance, not most of it. Negate it and attendance can still fall.
choices.negation: Not most of the attendees are older residents.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Whether there were better ways to save money doesn’t affect whether this cut lowers attendance.
choices.negation: The department could save as much money by ending some other program.

questions.stimulus: In one river, young salmon released from a hatchery survive to adulthood at a much lower rate than young salmon hatched in the wild. Hatchery salmon are fed by hand until their release and so have had little experience avoiding predators. Fisheries biologists therefore conclude that the hatchery salmon’s lower survival rate is due largely to their inexperience with predators.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the biologists’ argument?
choices: Wild salmon in the river are, on average, slightly larger at a given age than hatchery salmon are.
The number of predatory fish in the river has risen steadily over the past decade, according to a recent survey.
Some of the hatchery salmon released into the river survive to adulthood even though they were fed by hand.
Hatchery salmon are caught by anglers more often than wild salmon are, because anglers favor the stretch of river near the hatchery.
Hatchery salmon kept for a week in a pond stocked with pike before release later survived nearly as well as wild-hatched salmon.
questions.explanation: If inexperience with predators is the cause, giving hatchery salmon some predator experience should close the survival gap; (E) reports exactly that, without using the word ‘predator.’ (D) is tempting because it is about why hatchery salmon die, but it supplies a different cause (anglers), which weakens rather than strengthens the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Hatchery salmon survive less well mainly because they lack experience avoiding predators.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Hatchery salmon survive to adulthood less often than wild salmon; hatchery salmon are hand-fed and have little predator experience.

breakdown.analysis: Is predator inexperience really the cause? Hatchery fish differ from wild fish in lots of ways: size, genes, where they’re released. To strengthen a causal claim, look for an answer that isolates the proposed cause: change only the predator experience and see whether survival changes. It’s like testing whether a kid is failing math because he skips homework: make him do the homework and see whether his grades go up. We need an answer that says giving hatchery fish predator experience improves their survival.

choices.note: This points to a different difference between the groups: size. If anything it suggests another cause of the gap, so it doesn’t help the biologist.
More predators would affect wild and hatchery salmon alike. A survey of predator numbers doesn’t explain why one group survives worse than the other.
So? Some hatchery survivors are expected even if the group does worse overall. This says nothing about why the rates differ.
Tempting, because it’s about why hatchery salmon die. But it names a different cause, anglers near the hatchery. That’s an alternative explanation, so it weakens the argument.

CORRECT. Pike are predators, so a week with them gives these fish the experience the others lack. Same hatchery fish, plus that experience, and the survival gap nearly disappears. That points right at inexperience as the cause.

questions.stimulus: Last year the regional airline Talmor Air replaced the seats in its turboprop planes, which fly short mountain routes, with thinner, lighter seats. In surveys, passengers consistently rate the new seats as less comfortable than the old ones. Yet over the year after the change, Talmor’s passenger satisfaction scores for its turboprop flights rose substantially.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why Talmor’s satisfaction scores for its turboprop flights rose?
choices: Because the new seats are lighter, Talmor’s turboprops now rarely have to leave checked bags behind to meet their weight limits.
Talmor’s competitors on the same mountain routes did not replace the seats in their own turboprop planes that year.
Passengers on short flights generally care less about seat comfort than passengers on long flights do.
The new seats cost Talmor less to buy and maintain than the old seats did, which lowered its operating costs.
Satisfaction scores for Talmor’s jet flights, whose seats were not replaced, did not change at all over the same year.
questions.explanation: The lighter seats had a side benefit passengers notice: their bags now travel with them, which can outweigh a less comfortable seat on a short flight; (A) explains the rise. (C) is tempting, but caring less about comfort would at most keep scores from falling; it gives no reason for them to rise.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Talmor put in seats passengers find less comfortable, but satisfaction with its turboprop flights went up.

breakdown.analysis: How does a worse seat lead to happier passengers? Look for something else the new seats did. Here the clue is in the stimulus: the seats are lighter, and the planes fly short mountain routes. Weight might matter. The defect (thin seats) could come bundled with a benefit. We need an answer that shows the change produced some gain passengers value more than seat comfort.

choices.note: CORRECT. The lighter seats mean bags stop getting left behind. Passengers hate losing their bags more than they mind a thinner seat on a short hop, so satisfaction rises.
So? What competitors did doesn’t explain why Talmor’s own passengers became more satisfied with flights that got worse seats.
Tempting. It softens the blow of the worse seats. But ‘cares less’ only explains why scores might not drop much. It gives no reason for them to go up.
Wrong dimension. Lower costs for Talmor explain why the airline made the change, not why passengers were happier.
This makes the puzzle sharper, not smaller. It rules out a general rise across the airline but provides no explanation for the turboprop increase.

questions.stimulus: Customers at a small-town post office often wait twenty minutes or more in line during the lunch hour. To shorten these waits, the postmaster plans to staff a second service window during that hour. Since two clerks can serve customers twice as fast as one clerk can, the plan should cut lunch-hour waits roughly in half.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Most lunch-hour delays occur while parcels are weighed on the office’s single scale, which both of the windows would have to share.
Many customers who come to the post office during the lunch hour are buying only stamps, which takes a minute or two.
The clerk who would staff the second window currently sorts incoming mail in the back room during the lunch hour.
Customers at other post offices in the region report waiting in line for even longer than customers at this office do.
This post office has more customers during the lunch hour than during any other hour of the day.
questions.explanation: The prediction assumes that clerks are the bottleneck; A shows the real bottleneck is the single scale, which a second window can’t double, so waits won’t fall by half. C is tempting because it names a cost of the plan, but moving a sorting clerk says nothing about whether lines get shorter.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Adding a second window should cut lunch-hour waits roughly in half.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Two clerks can serve customers twice as fast as one.

breakdown.analysis: Two clerks serve twice as fast only if the clerk is what slows things down. What if something else is the choke point? Picture a grocery store that opens a second register but has only one bagger who has to bag every order. The lines barely move faster. We need an answer showing that the delay comes from something a second window doesn’t fix.

choices.note: CORRECT. If most of the wait is spent at the one scale, a second clerk just means two people waiting for the same scale. The doubling math breaks down.
If anything this helps. Quick stamp sales are exactly what an extra clerk speeds through. It doesn’t show the plan will fail.
Tempting, because it’s a real downside: the back room loses a sorter. But the argument is only about lunch-hour lines, and this doesn’t touch them.
Irrelevant comparison. Waits elsewhere being worse doesn’t tell us whether this postmaster’s plan will shorten this office’s lines.
This just confirms that lunch is the busy hour, which is why the plan targets it. It doesn’t show the extra window won’t help.

questions.stimulus: Under Wendmoor Insurance’s homeowner policy, a claim for water damage is paid only if the damage was reported within thirty days. Moreover, any claim for water damage caused by a burst pipe is paid in full, provided that the damage was reported within thirty days and the home’s pipes had been professionally inspected within the preceding five years. The Delgado family’s claim for water damage caused by a burst pipe was paid, but not in full.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: The Delgados reported the water damage to Wendmoor more than thirty days after it occurred.
Wendmoor pays claims in full only when the water damage was caused by a burst pipe.
The Delgados’ pipes had not been professionally inspected within the five years before the damage.
Some claims for water damage that was not caused by a burst pipe are paid in full by Wendmoor.
Wendmoor would have refused the Delgados’ claim entirely if their pipes had not been inspected within the preceding five years.
questions.explanation: Because the claim was paid at all, the damage was reported within thirty days; it was a burst pipe; so if the pipes had been inspected within five years it would have been paid in full. It wasn’t, so the inspection condition failed, as C says. A is the reversal trap: being paid proves the report was timely.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Water claim paid → reported within 30 days; 2. Burst pipe AND reported within 30 days AND inspected within 5 years → paid in full; 3. Delgados: burst pipe, claim paid, not in full.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Paid → reported within 30 days. So the Delgados reported on time. They had a burst pipe. Rule 2: burst pipe + on time + inspected → paid in full. Contrapositive: not paid in full → not burst pipe OR not on time OR not inspected. They had a burst pipe and reported on time, so the only condition left to fail is the inspection. We need: the pipes weren’t inspected within five years.

choices.note: This reverses the facts. The claim was paid, and payment requires a report within thirty days. So they must have reported on time.
We don’t know this. The policy gives one route to full payment; it never says burst pipes are the only route.
CORRECT. Burst pipe and an on-time report (proven by payment) plus an inspection would have guaranteed full payment. They didn’t get full payment, so the inspection piece is missing.
We don’t know this. The policy says nothing about full payment for other kinds of water damage. Could be true; doesn’t have to be.
Contradicted. Their pipes weren’t inspected, and their claim was still paid in part. So lacking an inspection doesn’t mean total refusal.

questions.stimulus: Business consultant: For most companies, replacing human telephone operators with an automated menu system is a false economy. Such systems do cut wage costs at first, which is why so many firms install them. But many callers who cannot quickly reach a person take their business elsewhere, and attracting a new customer generally costs a company far more than keeping an existing one. Savings that drive away customers who are costly to replace are not real savings.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion drawn in the business consultant’s argument?
choices: Many companies install automated telephone menus because such systems reduce their wage costs at first.
Most companies would not truly save money by switching from human operators to automated phone menus.
Savings that are achieved by driving away customers who are expensive to replace are not genuine savings.
Attracting a new customer generally costs a company more than keeping one of its existing customers does.
Companies should keep human operators on their telephone lines rather than install automated menu systems.
questions.explanation: The first sentence is the conclusion: for most companies, automated menus are a ‘false economy,’ meaning they don’t really save money. (B) says that in other words. (C) is the trap: the last sentence is a general claim offered to support the first, not the point the consultant is driving at.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: For most companies, replacing operators with an automated menu is a false economy.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Such systems cut wages at first (concession); callers who can’t reach a person leave; new customers cost more than keeping old ones; savings that drive off costly-to-replace customers aren’t real savings.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. ‘Such systems do cut wage costs’ is a concession; ‘But’ turns to the reasons; the last sentence is a general rule that ties the reasons back to the opening claim. Notice there is no ‘so’ or ‘thus’ anywhere, and the conclusion comes first. A ‘false economy’ is a cost cut that doesn’t actually save money. We need an answer that says automated menus don’t really save most companies money.

choices.note: Background plus a concession. The consultant grants that these systems cut wages at first and explains why firms buy them; that isn’t the point being argued.
CORRECT. ‘Would not truly save money’ is what ‘false economy’ means, and ‘most companies’ keeps the consultant’s scope. Everything else in the argument supports this.

Tempting. It’s the last sentence, it sounds like a verdict, and it’s nearly word for word. But it’s a general rule used to show that automated menus are a false economy. It supports the first sentence rather than the other way around.
A premise. It’s one of the reasons customers who leave are so costly; it supports the conclusion.
Goes beyond the argument. The consultant says automated menus don’t really save money, but never recommends what companies should do instead. ‘Not a real saving’ isn’t ‘should keep operators.’

questions.stimulus: In a recent study, researchers asked 200 adults to describe aloud the most stressful car trip they had ever taken, and they recorded the participants’ hand movements as they spoke. Seventy percent of the participants gestured with their hands at least once while doing so. This shows that recounting stressful experiences tends to make people gesture.
questions.stem: The argument’s reasoning is flawed in that the argument
choices: fails to establish how often the participants gesture when describing experiences that were not stressful
presumes, without providing justification, that the participants found the trips they described to be equally stressful
takes for granted that any participant who gestured while describing the trip was feeling stressed while doing so
takes for granted that people remember the details of stressful experiences accurately when they describe them
confuses a possible cause of gesturing while speaking with a possible effect of gesturing while speaking
questions.explanation: To show that stressful memories in particular bring out gesturing, the argument needs a baseline: if people gesture just as often describing their grocery list, the stress did nothing. (A) names the missing comparison. (C) is tempting because it sounds like the argument’s link between stress and gesturing, but the argument never treats gesturing as a sign that a speaker is stressed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Recounting stressful experiences tends to make people gesture.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 70 percent of 200 adults gestured at least once while describing their most stressful car trip.

breakdown.analysis: Seventy percent gestured. Compared to what? Most people wave their hands around when they talk about anything. If 70 percent also gesture when describing breakfast, stress has nothing to do with it. This is a missing comparison group: the study only looked at one kind of story. It’s like noting that most people blink while watching horror movies and concluding horror movies make people blink. We need an answer that points to the missing baseline.

choices.note: CORRECT. Without knowing how often people gesture when talking about non-stressful things, 70 percent tells us nothing about stress. That’s the missing baseline.
Irrelevant. The trips don’t have to be equally stressful. The conclusion is about stressful stories in general, not about matching stress levels.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Everyone in the race finished, so all the runners must be equally fit.

choices.note: Tempting, because it links stress and gesturing the way the argument does. But it runs the link backward. The argument says recounting stress produces gestures; it never infers from a gesture that the speaker felt stressed, so it takes nothing like this for granted.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Maria is waving her hands as she talks, so she must be upset about something.

choices.note: Memory accuracy doesn’t matter. The study measured gesturing while people talked, which happens whether or not their memories are correct.
Describes a different flaw. The argument doesn’t mix up cause and effect; no one suggests gesturing causes stressful memories.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: People who carry umbrellas get rained on more, so carrying umbrellas causes rain.

questions.stimulus: Agricultural adviser: In field trials over three growing seasons, plots planted with the wheat variety Dunmore yielded 15 percent more grain per hectare than plots planted with Selby Red, the variety that farmers in the Selby Valley now grow. The trials were run on soils like those of the valley. So Selby Valley farmers who switch from Selby Red to Dunmore will earn more from their wheat crops.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the adviser’s argument?
choices: Selby Valley farmers have grown Selby Red for several generations, and many of them are reluctant to change varieties.
In each of the three trial seasons, rainfall in the trial area was close to the long-term average for the Selby Valley.
Dunmore’s yield advantage over Selby Red was smaller in the driest of the three trial seasons than in the other two.
Wheat prices in the region have fallen over the past several years, and most analysts expect them to keep falling.
Valley mills pay about a quarter less per tonne for Dunmore grain than for Selby Red, because Dunmore is lower in protein.
questions.explanation: The trials show more grain per hectare, but the conclusion is about earnings, which depend on price as well as yield. (E) says Dunmore grain sells for about a quarter less per tonne, which more than cancels a 15 percent yield gain. (D) is tempting, but falling prices hit both varieties alike, so it doesn’t affect whether switching pays.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Selby Valley farmers who switch to Dunmore will earn more from their wheat.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In trials on valley-like soils, Dunmore yielded 15 percent more grain per hectare than Selby Red.

breakdown.analysis: So what if it yields more grain? More grain isn’t more money. Earnings depend on how much you grow AND what each tonne sells for (and what it costs to grow). The adviser jumps from a yield fact to an earnings conclusion. That’s a scope shift: yield → income. We need an answer that says Dunmore loses on some other part of the earnings picture, enough to wipe out its yield edge. Quick math helps: 15 percent more grain at a quarter less per tonne is 1.15 × 0.75, about 0.86. Less money, not more.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether farmers want to switch says nothing about whether those who do switch will earn more. The conclusion is about switchers.
This helps the argument. Normal rainfall means the trial conditions match the valley, so the yield result is more likely to carry over.
So? Smaller is still an advantage. Dunmore beat Selby Red in every season described, so this doesn’t undercut the claim that switchers will do better.
Tempting, because falling prices mean lower earnings. But they fall for both varieties. The question is whether Dunmore beats Selby Red, and a price drop that hits both leaves that comparison alone.

CORRECT. Earnings are yield times price. Dunmore gives 15 percent more grain, but each tonne fetches about a quarter less, so a Dunmore hectare brings in roughly 86 percent of what a Selby Red hectare does. Switching would cost farmers money.

questions.stimulus: In the Kaleni language, a word borrowed from another language keeps its original stress pattern for at least a generation after it enters Kaleni. Every native Kaleni word, by contrast, is stressed on its first syllable. The common Kaleni word “kelmaro” is stressed on its second syllable.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The word “kelmaro” entered the Kaleni language at some point within the past generation.
Most words borrowed into Kaleni are stressed on their second syllable.
“Kelmaro” was borrowed from a language in which it was stressed on its second syllable.
The word “kelmaro” is not one that originated within the Kaleni language itself.
Borrowed words that have been part of Kaleni for more than a generation are stressed on their first syllable.
questions.explanation: Native words are always stressed on the first syllable; “kelmaro” is not, so it cannot be native, as (D) says. (A) and (E) misread ‘at least a generation’: borrowed words keep their stress for a generation or longer, so a word stressed on its second syllable may have been borrowed long ago, and nothing says older borrowings shift.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Borrowed word → keeps original stress for at least a generation; 2. Native Kaleni word → stressed on first syllable; 3. “Kelmaro” is stressed on its second syllable.

breakdown.analysis: Start with the cleanest rule. Native → first-syllable stress. Contrapositive: not first-syllable stress → not native. Kelmaro is stressed on the second syllable, so it isn’t native. Done. Watch the phrase ‘at least a generation.’ It sets a minimum, not a maximum. It doesn’t say what happens after a generation, so answers about timing or later stress changes are unsupported.

choices.note: Tempting. It feels like a borrowed word that still has odd stress must be recent. But ‘at least a generation’ means borrowed words may keep their stress much longer. Kelmaro could be centuries old.
We don’t know this. One second-syllable word tells us nothing about most borrowed words.

We don’t know this. Kelmaro isn’t native, but if it was borrowed long ago its stress could have shifted, and it might not even be borrowed (it could, for example, have been formed some other way). Its original stress is unknown.
CORRECT. Native words are always first-syllable stressed. Kelmaro isn’t, so it isn’t native: it didn’t originate in Kaleni. This one actually must be true.
Reads a maximum into a minimum. The stimulus never says borrowed words shift after a generation; they keep their stress for at least that long, maybe forever.

questions.stimulus: School board member: The district’s cafeteria vendor has proposed adding flavored milk to the lunch menu, noting that students would drink more milk if it were offered. Flavored milk does supply calcium, which growing children need. But it also contains a considerable amount of added sugar, and many parents, worried about their children’s health, have told the board they do not want sugary drinks offered at school. So we should decline the vendor’s proposal.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the school board member’s reasoning?
choices: One should not change what one offers children merely because the change would lead them to consume more of something.
A school should offer a sweetened drink only if offering it will not lead students to drink fewer unsweetened beverages.
Decisions about what a school serves should rest solely on nutrition, never on the preferences that parents express.
One should not provide children with something many of their parents oppose on health grounds, even if it would benefit them somewhat.
A school should offer any food that supplies a nutrient that children need, unless there is reason to think that students would refuse to eat it.
questions.explanation: The board member grants the calcium benefit but lets the parents’ health worries about sugar decide. (D) says, in general terms, not to provide children with something many parents oppose on health grounds even if it benefits the children somewhat, which yields ‘decline.’ (A) is the trap: it rejects the vendor’s reason for adding the milk, but rejecting a reason to do something isn’t a reason not to do it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The board should decline the vendor’s flavored-milk proposal.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Flavored milk supplies needed calcium (concession), but it has lots of added sugar and many parents, worried about health, oppose sugary drinks at school.

breakdown.analysis: The board member weighs two things: calcium on one side, sugar plus parents’ health worries on the other, and lets the second win. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, triggered by facts the stimulus actually gives. So we need a rule like: when many parents object on health grounds, that beats nutritional value. Watch for principles whose ‘if’ part depends on a fact we don’t have.

choices.note: Tempting. It knocks down the vendor’s reason (students would drink more). But ‘don’t change it merely because they’d consume more’ doesn’t say ‘don’t change it.’ There could be other reasons, like the calcium. It never gets you to ‘decline.’

Tempting, since it’s about sweetened drinks and reads like a rule. But it bars the drink only if it would cut into students’ unsweetened drinking, and nothing in the argument says it would. Its condition isn’t shown to be met.
Opposite direction. The board member’s reasoning leans on parents’ concerns; this principle would forbid exactly that.

CORRECT. Flavored milk is something many parents oppose for health reasons (the sugar), and it would do some good (the calcium). The principle says don’t provide it anyway, so the board should decline. It’s phrased generally, ‘something’ and ‘benefit them somewhat,’ but it covers this case.
Wrong verdict. Flavored milk supplies calcium, and the vendor says students would drink it, so this principle says to offer it. It cuts against the board member.

questions.stimulus: In one city, homes equipped with smoke detectors that are wired into the house’s electrical system are more likely to suffer serious fire damage than are homes that have only battery-powered detectors. Yet the city’s fire officials insist that wired detectors are more reliable than battery-powered ones and that nearly every home would be safer with them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Battery-powered detectors in the city’s homes are often found during inspections to have dead or missing batteries.
Wired detectors cost considerably more to install than battery-powered detectors do, though they cost less to maintain over time.
In homes with wired detectors that have suffered serious fire damage, the alarms usually sounded well before firefighters arrived.
Most serious house fires in the city begin at night, when residents are asleep and depend on a detector’s alarm to wake them.
The city requires wired detectors in every home with a wood stove or fireplace, the source of most serious house fires there.
questions.explanation: If wired detectors are required precisely in the homes most prone to serious fires, those homes would suffer more damage even if the detectors work better, so (E) lets both facts stand. (C) is tempting because it shows the wired alarms work, but that only backs the officials; it gives no reason the wired-detector homes fare worse.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Homes with wired detectors suffer more serious fire damage, but officials say wired detectors are more reliable and would make homes safer.

breakdown.analysis: How can the better detector go with worse outcomes? Ask who has the wired detectors. If they’re installed mostly in homes that are far more likely to catch fire, those homes could have more damage even though the detector helps. It’s like noticing that people with the best doctors are often the sickest: the sick people seek out the best doctors. We need an answer that shows the wired-detector homes differ in fire risk. Watch for answers that explain only one side.

choices.note: This deepens the puzzle. If battery detectors often don’t work, the homes relying on them should do worse, not better.
Wrong dimension. Installation and maintenance costs say nothing about fire damage or reliability.

Tempting, because it seems to explain the damage away: the alarms worked, so the detectors aren’t to blame. But that only supports the officials. It gives no reason why homes with working wired alarms would suffer more damage than other homes. If anything, it deepens the puzzle.
This applies to every home, wired or not. A fact about all homes can’t explain a difference between two groups of them.
CORRECT. Wired detectors are concentrated in the riskiest homes. Those homes have more serious fires to begin with, so they show more damage even if the detectors are better. Both facts survive.

questions.stimulus: Choir director: The Oldham Choral Society should keep holding its concerts at St. Bride’s Hall. Some members want to move them to the new civic auditorium, which seats twice as many people. But our audiences have never filled even St. Bride’s, and the auditorium’s acoustics flatten unamplified voices. Thus, a move would leave the choir sounding worse to no more listeners than before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the choir director’s argument by the claim that a move would leave the choir sounding worse to no more listeners than before?
choices: It is the overall conclusion that the choir director’s argument as a whole is intended to establish.
It is a premise that some members of the society offer in support of moving the concerts to the auditorium.
It is a general principle that the choir director applies to the particular case of the society’s concerts.
It is a conclusion drawn from other claims in the argument and offered in support of its main conclusion.
It is a claim that the choir director concedes is true but argues is outweighed by other considerations.
questions.explanation: The claim is drawn (‘Thus’) from the facts about audience size and acoustics, and it in turn supports the opening recommendation to stay at St. Bride’s, so (D) is right. (A) is the trap: the ‘Thus’ marks a conclusion, but not the main one; the claim is the reason the society should keep its concerts where they are.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The society should keep holding its concerts at St. Bride’s Hall.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Audiences never fill St. Bride’s and the auditorium flattens voices; so a move would mean worse sound for no more listeners (the claim in question).

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The claim starts with ‘Thus,’ so it’s a conclusion of something: the facts about audiences and acoustics. But does the argument stop there? No. Why should the society stay? Because moving would make it sound worse to the same crowd. So the claim supports the first sentence. Chain: audience and acoustics facts → worse sound, no more listeners → stay at St. Bride’s. That makes it an intermediate conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting, because of the ‘Thus.’ But the main conclusion sits in the first sentence with no indicator: keep the concerts at St. Bride’s. This claim is the reason for it.
Wrong side. The members who want to move would never say the move makes the choir sound worse. This is the director’s own claim against them.
It’s about one specific move for one choir. That’s a particular claim, not a general principle.
CORRECT. It’s supported by the audience and acoustics facts, and it supports the recommendation to stay. Drawn from premises, used as a premise.
The director doesn’t concede this; the director asserts it and relies on it. Nothing outweighs it.

questions.stimulus: Public works director: Some council members want to ban heavy trucks from the city’s residential streets to reduce the damage those streets suffer each year. Granted, a ban would prevent some of that damage. But our inspection records show that most of the damage to residential streets is caused by water freezing and thawing beneath the pavement, not by the weight of passing vehicles. So a truck ban would not be worth enacting.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the public works director’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: fails to consider the possibility that banning heavy trucks would reduce at least some of the damage to the city’s residential streets
draws a conclusion about all of the city’s streets from inspection records that concern only its residential streets
treats repairing freeze-thaw damage and banning heavy trucks as though the city could pursue only one of the two
takes for granted that a measure is not worth adopting unless it targets whatever causes the greater part of a problem
presumes, without providing justification, that the inspection records correctly identify the cause of the damage to each street
questions.explanation: The director concedes the ban would prevent some damage but rejects it because trucks aren’t the main cause. That only works if a measure must attack the biggest cause to be worthwhile, which is (D). (A) is the trap: the director explicitly grants that the ban would prevent some damage, so the argument doesn’t overlook that.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A truck ban on residential streets would not be worth enacting.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A ban would prevent some damage (concession); but most damage comes from freeze-thaw, not vehicle weight.

breakdown.analysis: So what if trucks aren’t the main cause? A fix can be worth it even if it handles only a minor cause, especially if it’s cheap. It’s like refusing to fix a dripping faucet because most of your water bill comes from the lawn sprinkler. We need an answer that says the director takes for granted that only a remedy aimed at the biggest cause is worth adopting. Watch for answers that accuse the director of missing something the director actually concedes.

choices.note: Tempting. It sounds like the obvious objection. But the director says it outright: ‘Granted, a ban would prevent some of that damage.’ You can’t fail to consider what you concede. The problem is what the director does with that concession.
Scope mismatch that isn’t there. The records and the conclusion are both about residential streets; the argument never says anything about the city’s other streets.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our records on downtown streets show little truck damage, so trucks do little damage anywhere in the city.

choices.note: A real flaw this argument doesn’t commit. The director never proposes freeze-thaw repairs as an alternative, so nothing is treated as either-or.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We can either fix the drainage or ban trucks, and the drainage matters more, so no ban.

choices.note: CORRECT. The ban helps, by the director’s own admission, but is dismissed because it doesn’t target the main cause. That rejection works only if a remedy must tackle the bigger share of a problem to be worth adopting.
A premise objection. Any argument relies on its evidence being accurate; that isn’t a flaw in the reasoning. Even with perfect records the conclusion still wouldn’t follow.

questions.stimulus: Every study planned for the research ship’s spring voyage depends on its deep-water sonar. A study that depends on the sonar can be carried out only if the sonar’s cracked housing is repaired before the ship sails. So unless the housing is repaired before the ship sails, none of the studies planned for the spring voyage can be carried out.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every dish on tonight’s tasting menu calls for fresh saffron. A dish that calls for saffron can be served only if the delayed saffron shipment arrives by noon. So if the shipment arrives by noon, every dish on tonight’s tasting menu can be served.

Some of the songs on the band’s new album were recorded in the old studio. A song recorded there can be released only if the studio’s owner consents. So unless the owner consents, none of the songs on the band’s new album can be released.

Every runner on the team trains on the school track, and the track can be used only if it has been resurfaced since the winter. The track has now been resurfaced. So every runner on the team will be able to use the track this season.

As long as the city’s emissions ban stays in place, Mira’s delivery vans will be kept out of the old town, since the ban bars every diesel vehicle from the old town and every van in Mira’s fleet runs on diesel.

Every apartment in the Marlow Building has a gas stove, and a gas stove can be installed only by a licensed fitter. So every licensed fitter in the city must have installed at least one of the stoves in the Marlow Building.
questions.explanation: The argument runs: all X are Y; a Y can happen only if R; so without R, no X can happen. (D) has that form with the conclusion first and the conditions reworded (‘as long as the ban stays’ = unless it is lifted; ‘bars every diesel vehicle’ = a diesel may enter only if the ban ends). (A) copies the original’s sentence frames but turns a necessary condition into a sufficient one; (B) swaps ‘every’ for ‘some.’

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Unless the housing is repaired before sailing, none of the planned studies can be carried out.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every planned study depends on the sonar; a sonar study can be done only if the housing is repaired.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All X are Y; Y → requires R; so not R → no X.

breakdown.analysis: Write the skeleton: every planned study (X) needs the sonar (Y). Any Y requires R (repair). So no R → no X. It’s valid: if R is required for every Y, and every X is a Y, then R is required for every X. Match the skeleton, not the words. The trap here is an answer that copies the original’s sentences (‘Every… only if… So…’) but changes one piece of logic. The right answer hides by putting its conclusion first and saying ‘as long as’ and ‘bars’ instead of ‘unless’ and ‘only if.’

choices.note: Tempting, because its sentences line up with the original’s almost word for word. But it concludes that the shipment arriving GUARANTEES service. ‘Only if’ gives a necessary condition, not a sufficient one, so this reasoning is flawed and the original isn’t.

Tempting, and close. But ‘some of the songs’ were recorded there, not all. With ‘some,’ the conclusion that NONE can be released doesn’t follow; songs recorded elsewhere might be fine. One quantifier changes the structure.

Different structure. It affirms the necessary condition (the track was resurfaced) and concludes the runners can use it, treating a requirement as a guarantee. The original never says the condition is met.
CORRECT. Ban in place → no diesel enters; every van is diesel; so while the ban stays, no van enters. That’s ‘unless R, no X’ with the order flipped and the conditions reworded.
This flips the ‘all’: every stove needs a fitter doesn’t mean every fitter worked on a stove. A different, flawed structure.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: Any pottery fragment that bears traces of lead glaze was made after the end of the Varn period, since potters in this region learned lead glazing only from traders who arrived at the very end of that period. The pottery fragments found in the lowest layer of the dig at Osk Hill bear traces of lead glaze. Therefore, the lowest layer at Osk Hill was deposited after the Varn period ended.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the archaeologist’s argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any layer of a dig that was deposited after the end of the Varn period contains at least some pottery made after that period ended.
Pottery fragments found in the lowest layer of a dig are usually the oldest fragments found anywhere at that dig.
No layer of a dig that was deposited before the end of the Varn period contains any pottery that was made after that period ended.
The traders who introduced lead glazing to the region settled at Osk Hill near the end of the Varn period.
No pottery made during the Varn period has been found in any of the layers of the dig at Osk Hill.
questions.explanation: The premises establish only that the lowest layer’s fragments were made after the Varn period. (C) says that no layer laid down before the period ended holds post-Varn pottery; by contrapositive, a layer that does hold such pottery was deposited after the period ended, which is the conclusion. (A) is the near-miss: it runs the same link backward, from the layer’s date to the pottery, so it guarantees nothing.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The lowest layer at Osk Hill was deposited after the Varn period.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lead-glazed fragment → made after the Varn period; the lowest layer’s fragments are lead-glazed.

breakdown.analysis: Chain what we have: lowest-layer fragments → lead-glazed → made after Varn. But the conclusion is about when the layer was deposited, not when the pottery was made. Could fragments made later get into an older layer? Burrowing animals, later digging. The missing link is: layer contains post-Varn pottery → layer deposited after Varn. The right answer states it backward, as a contrapositive: deposited before the end of Varn → no post-Varn pottery. Flip it and you get the bridge. Full chain: lowest-layer fragments → glazed → made after Varn → (assumption, contrapositive) layer not deposited before Varn ended. Watch for an answer that links the same two ideas in the wrong direction.

choices.note: Tempting, because it uses exactly the right two ideas. But it runs the wrong way: deposited after Varn → contains post-Varn pottery. We need contains post-Varn pottery → deposited after Varn. Knowing that later layers hold later pottery says nothing about whether an earlier layer might too.
Tempting, since it’s about the lowest layer. But ‘usually the oldest’ doesn’t tell us the layer was laid down after the fragments were made, and ‘usually’ can’t guarantee anything.

CORRECT. Deposited before Varn ended → no post-Varn pottery. Contrapositive: contains post-Varn pottery → not deposited before Varn ended, i.e., deposited after. The lowest layer contains such pottery, so the conclusion follows.
Irrelevant. Where the traders lived doesn’t connect the fragments’ date to the layer’s date.
So? Finding no Varn-period pottery doesn’t show when the lowest layer was deposited. The layer could still predate the glazed fragments that ended up in it.

questions.stimulus: Five years ago an auto insurer began requiring every newly insured driver under twenty to have a dashboard monitor that beeps whenever the driver brakes harshly or accelerates sharply. Since then, the number of accident claims the insurer receives per young driver it insures has fallen by a quarter. The insurer’s analysts conclude that the monitors have made its young drivers safer.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the analysts’ argument?
choices: How much does it cost the insurer to supply and install a dashboard monitor in each young driver’s car?
Do the young drivers who have the monitor say that its beeping has made them more careful about how they brake?
Have claims per young driver fallen by a similar amount at insurers that do not require the monitor?
Are drivers under twenty involved in more accidents per mile driven than drivers over twenty are, on average?
Do many of the young drivers whom the insurer covers drive cars that are owned by their parents rather than by themselves?
questions.explanation: Claims fell after the monitors arrived, but young drivers’ claims might have fallen everywhere, from safer cars or other trends. (C) asks for that comparison: if other insurers saw no similar drop, the monitor looks responsible; if they saw the same drop, it doesn’t. (D) is the trap: it is a true-sounding fact about young drivers that bears on no change over time.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The monitors have made the insurer’s young drivers safer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the insurer began requiring the monitors five years ago, claims per young driver have fallen by a quarter.

breakdown.analysis: Before and after, but compared to what? Lots of things changed in five years: cars got more safety features, maybe gas prices kept teens off the road. If young drivers’ claims dropped just as much at insurers with no monitors, the monitor did nothing special. We need a two-sided question about that comparison: one answer helps the argument, the other hurts it.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Cost bears on whether the program is worth it, not on whether the monitors made anyone safer.

Tempting, because it’s about the monitor’s effect. But it’s one-sided and weak: drivers can be wrong about what changed their habits, and the claims data already tell us claims fell. Self-reports don’t show the monitor caused the drop.

CORRECT. Yes: the drop happened everywhere, so something other than the monitor likely explains it. No: only this insurer’s young drivers improved, which points to the monitor. Either answer moves the argument.
Tempting, because it sounds like a base rate. But it compares young and older drivers at one moment; it says nothing about why young drivers’ claims fell over time.
Irrelevant. Who owns the car doesn’t affect whether the monitor changed how the young drivers drive.

questions.stimulus: Linguist: It is often said that text messaging is eroding young people’s ability to spell, since their messages are full of abbreviations such as “thx” and “l8r.” But to shorten a word deliberately in such ways, a writer must know how the full word is normally spelled and how it sounds. And studies find that the students who use such abbreviations most often tend to score at least as well on spelling tests as students who rarely use them. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the linguist’s argument?
choices: young people today spell at least as well as young people did before text messaging became common
the abbreviations found in young people’s text messages give little reason to think that texting harms their spelling
young people who rarely use texting abbreviations are less likely than frequent users to know how full words are normally spelled
young people who abbreviate words in their text messages do so deliberately rather than because they cannot spell the full words
students who rarely use texting abbreviations would become better spellers if they began to use them more often
questions.explanation: The linguist attacks the evidence behind the popular claim: deliberate abbreviation requires knowing the full spelling, and heavy abbreviators spell at least as well as others. So the abbreviations are poor evidence of eroded spelling, which is (B). (A) borrows “at least as well” but switches the comparison to one across time, which the studies never make. (C) borrows the premise’s wording but turns it around.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (blank) The linguist’s response to the claim that texting erodes spelling.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Deliberate shortening requires knowing the full spelling and sound; heavy abbreviators score at least as well on spelling tests as light ones.

breakdown.analysis: What is the linguist pushing back on? Not the idea that texting could ever affect spelling, but the evidence offered for it: ‘their messages are full of abbreviations.’ Both premises say abbreviations don’t show poor spelling. So the blank should say the abbreviations are weak evidence. Watch the strength: ‘at least as well’ isn’t ‘better,’ and weakening someone’s evidence isn’t disproving their claim.

choices.note: Tempting, because it borrows “at least as well” from the premise. But the studies compare heavy and light abbreviators today, not today’s young people with an earlier generation. This changes the comparison. Nothing in the passage is about spelling over time.

CORRECT. Abbreviating deliberately requires knowing the spelling, and heavy abbreviators spell fine. So the abbreviations themselves don’t support the erosion claim. That’s a modest conclusion both premises point to.

Tempting, because it reuses the linguist’s language about knowing how full words are spelled. But the premise says only that deliberate abbreviators must know the spelling; it says nothing about what people who rarely abbreviate know. And ‘at least as well’ allows the two groups to spell equally well.
Unsupported. The linguist says what deliberate shortening requires, but never says that every abbreviation in young people’s messages is deliberate. This turns a conditional into a fact.
A causal leap. Nothing shows that abbreviating improves spelling, let alone that starting would help the students who rarely do it.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, seagrass meadows along one stretch of coast have shrunk most sharply near the coast’s three desalination plants, which discharge a warm, highly salty brine into nearby waters. Seagrass is known to be harmed by unusually salty water. So the increased salinity of the water near the plants is probably the main cause of the meadows’ decline there.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the argument EXCEPT:
choices: Seagrass is also harmed by water that is unusually warm, and the brine raises the temperature of the water near the plants.
Near a coastal power station that discharges water that is warm but not unusually salty, the seagrass meadows have not shrunk.
The meadows near the plants had been stable in extent for many years before the plants began discharging their brine.
Water samples taken near the plants show salinity well above the level at which seagrass growth is known to slow.
Boats, whose anchors can tear up seagrass, anchor no more often near the plants than they do elsewhere along the coast.
questions.explanation: The brine is both salty and warm, so the argument needs heat and other factors not to be the culprit. (B) rules out heat, (C) fixes the timing, (D) shows the salinity is high enough to harm, and (E) rules out anchoring. (A) does the reverse: it offers warmth as a rival cause, so it doesn’t support salinity as the main cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Increased salinity near the plants is probably the main cause of the seagrass decline there.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Meadows shrank most near plants that discharge warm, salty brine; seagrass is harmed by unusually salty water.

breakdown.analysis: Four answers help and one doesn’t. Find the odd one out. The brine is two things at once: salty and warm. So the argument picks salinity over heat without saying why. Strengtheners will rule out heat or other causes, or show the salt is really there and the timing fits. The answer we want either does nothing or points to a rival cause. Careful: an answer that blames the plants for a different reason does not support blaming salt.

choices.note: CORRECT. It blames the plants, which feels supportive, but it blames them through heat, not salt. That’s a rival explanation for the decline, so it weakens the claim that salinity is the main cause.
Strengthens. Warm water without extra salt left the seagrass alone, so heat alone doesn’t seem to do it. That leaves salt as the likely culprit.
Strengthens. The decline began only after the brine did, which fits the plants as the cause and rules out a decline already under way.
Strengthens. The salinity near the plants is actually high enough to harm seagrass, so the proposed cause is really present at harmful levels.
Strengthens, though it looks irrelevant at first. Anchors are a possible rival cause, and this shows they aren’t concentrated near the plants, so they can’t explain why the decline is sharpest there.

questions.stimulus: A survey of households in one town found that households that own a dog report knowing, on average, twice as many of their neighbors by name as households without a dog report knowing. Walking a dog brings people into frequent, casual contact with the neighbors they pass. So owning a dog leads people to become acquainted with more of their neighbors.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Dog owners in the town who walk their dogs several times a day know more of their neighbors by name than do dog owners who seldom walk them.
Residents of the town who own cats report knowing about as many of their neighbors by name as do residents who own no pets at all.
Most dog owners in the town learned of their dogs through neighbors, so residents who know few neighbors seldom hear of a dog needing a home.
Dog owners in the town say that many of the neighbors they know by name are other dog owners whom they first met while out walking.
Residents who have lived in the town for many years know more of their neighbors by name than newer residents do, whether or not they own a dog.
questions.explanation: (C) says that in this town people usually find a dog through their neighbors, so knowing many neighbors makes a person more likely to end up with a dog. That lets the survey’s link run the other way: knowing neighbors leads to dog ownership, not the reverse. (E) is the trap: it names another factor, but nothing says dog owners have lived in town longer. (D) and (A) actually fit the walking mechanism.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Owning a dog leads people to become acquainted with more of their neighbors.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Dog-owning households report knowing twice as many neighbors by name as households without dogs; walking a dog brings people into contact with neighbors.

breakdown.analysis: Which came first, the dog or the neighbors? The survey shows only that the two go together. The argument reads it as dog → neighbors, through walking. But if people who already know their neighbors are the ones who end up with dogs, the correlation runs the other way. The right answer won’t say ‘reverse causation’; it will describe a situation that implies it. Watch for alternative factors that aren’t tied to dog ownership, and for facts that actually fit the walking story.

choices.note: Supports the argument. More walking, more names: that fits the proposed mechanism. A rushed reader sees ‘know more’ and stops thinking.
Tempting, since it seems to show pets don’t matter. But cats aren’t walked past the neighbors, so the argument predicts exactly this. It’s consistent with the argument, not a weakener.

CORRECT. It reads like a stray fact about how people find dogs. But it means people who know lots of neighbors are the ones who hear of dogs and end up owning them. So the survey’s pattern could come from neighbors → dog, not dog → neighbors. That gives the correlation a cause running in the opposite direction.
Tempting, because it’s about how owners know their neighbors. But meeting people while out walking is exactly the argument’s mechanism, so this supports the argument.

Tempting. It’s a real alternative factor: length of residence. But it works only if dog owners have lived in town longer, and nothing says so. ‘Whether or not they own a dog’ tells you tenure matters in both groups, not that it differs between them.

questions.stimulus: A regional health authority’s annual report states that at each of the region’s five hospitals, the average length of a patient’s stay was shorter last year than it had been the year before. The authority’s director concludes that the average length of a patient’s stay across all five hospitals taken together must also have been shorter last year than the year before.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the director’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that the average length of stay fell by the same amount at each of the five hospitals
fails to consider that the average stay across the region could have fallen even if it had risen at some of the five hospitals
infers that each hospital treated fewer patients last year from the fact that patients at each hospital stayed for shorter periods
overlooks the possibility that the proportion of the region’s patients treated at each of the hospitals changed from one year to the next
treats a decline in the average length of patients’ stays as though it showed an improvement in the quality of the patients’ care
questions.explanation: An overall average depends on how patients are spread across the hospitals, not just on each hospital’s average. If last year many more patients went to the hospital with the longest stays, the regional average could rise even though every hospital’s fell. (D) names that overlooked shift. (B) sounds similar but describes a way the conclusion could be true, which is no criticism of the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The average stay across all five hospitals together must have been shorter last year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: At each of the five hospitals, the average stay was shorter last year than the year before.

breakdown.analysis: Every part improved, so the whole improved? Not with averages. Picture two hospitals. The first, a long-stay specialist hospital, drops from 10 days to 9; the second drops from 3 days to 2. Year one: 10 patients at the first, 90 at the second, so the average is (100 + 270)/100 = 3.7 days. Year two: 90 at the first, 10 at the second, so (810 + 20)/100 = 8.3 days. Both averages fell; the combined average more than doubled. The weights changed. This is a classic statistics trap (Simpson’s paradox); know it. We need an answer about the mix of patients across hospitals shifting.

choices.note: Tempting, because equal drops sound like what you’d need. But they aren’t needed: the averages can fall by different amounts and the overall average will still fall as long as the patient mix stays put. The argument doesn’t rely on this.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Every store raised prices, so each must have raised them by 5 percent, just as the flagship did.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a subtle point about averages. But it’s about how the conclusion could be true by another route. That doesn’t weaken an argument that the conclusion must be true; it isn’t a flaw at all.
The director makes no claim about how many patients each hospital treated. Shorter stays don’t imply fewer patients, and the argument never says they do.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Each customer spent less time in the store, so the store must have had fewer customers.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the share of patients going to each hospital changed, say toward the long-stay hospital, the combined average can rise even though every hospital’s average fell. The director ignores the weights.
A different flaw. The director concludes nothing about quality of care, only about average length of stay.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Patients went home sooner this year, so the hospital must be giving them better care.

questions.stimulus: All of the films nominated for this year’s Brennan Prize are documentaries. About half of the films shown at this year’s Leland Festival are documentaries.
