And some of this year’s documentaries received funding from the National Arts Council. So some films that received Arts Council funding were nominated for the Brennan Prize, and some were shown at the Leland Festival.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Every member of the chess club also belongs to the math club, and most members of the math club are seniors. So most members of the chess club are seniors, and so are some members of the math club.

All of the paintings in the museum’s east gallery are oil paintings, and about half of those in its west gallery are. Every oil painting in the museum is insured. So all of the east gallery’s paintings and at least half of the west gallery’s paintings are insured.

Some of the volunteers at the animal shelter are teachers, and some of the teachers in town donate money to the shelter. So some of the shelter’s volunteers donate money to the shelter, and some of its donors are teachers.

All of the novels on this year’s prize shortlist were written in English, as were about half of the novels in the town library. So about half of the novels in the town library are on this year’s prize shortlist.

Some of the restaurants that won a city health award must be on Pine Street and some must be in the harbor district, for several award winners serve vegetarian dishes, as do all Pine Street restaurants and nearly fifty percent of the harbor district’s.
questions.explanation: The original has: all W are Y; about half of X are Y; some Y are Z; so some Z are W and some Z are X. It ignores that the Y’s that are Z might be neither W’s nor X’s. (E) has the same structure, with the conclusion first and the premises reordered and reworded. (B) is the dominant trap: it opens exactly like the original, but its third premise says every oil painting is insured, so its conclusion follows and it is valid. (C) commits a different some–some error with only two groups.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some Arts Council–funded films were Brennan nominees, and some were shown at Leland.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All Brennan nominees are documentaries; about half of Leland films are documentaries; some documentaries got Arts Council funding.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All W are Y; about half of X are Y; some Y are Z; so some Z are W and some Z are X.

breakdown.analysis: Why is this bad? The funded documentaries could be ones that were neither nominated nor shown at Leland. Picture 100 documentaries this year: 5 nominated, 10 at Leland, and the 3 funded ones among the other 85. ‘Some Y are Z’ doesn’t say WHICH Y’s. This is the overlap fallacy: two groups that both sit inside a bigger group needn’t overlap with a third slice of it. Most students pick (B), because its first two sentences are a near-copy of the original’s. It fails because its third premise says EVERY oil painting is insured, and ‘every’ guarantees the result, so (B) is valid. The right answer (E) hides by reordering: it states its conclusion first, puts the ‘some’ premise ahead of the others, and says ‘several’ and ‘nearly fifty percent,’ but the pieces are identical.

choices.note: A different flaw: all chess members are math members; most math members are seniors; so most chess members are seniors. That’s the all-plus-most error, without the original’s two-part ‘some’ conclusion.

Tempting. It opens exactly like the original. But its third premise is ‘every oil painting is insured,’ not ‘some.’ That makes the conclusion follow, so this argument is valid and can’t match a flawed one.
Only two groups and a ‘some … some’ chain: some volunteers are teachers, some teachers donate. A different error, missing the all / about-half structure.
A different flaw: it concludes that half the library is on the shortlist just because both groups contain English novels. There’s no third ‘some’ group and no two-part conclusion.

CORRECT. Conclusion first, then the reasons. Several award winners (Z) serve vegetarian dishes (Y); every Pine Street restaurant (W) and nearly fifty percent of the harbor restaurants (X) do too; so some award winners are W’s and some are X’s. Same overlap error, with the order and wording changed.

questions.stimulus: School district policy: A student may be excused from the physical education requirement only if a parent or guardian submits a written request. Once such a request is submitted, any student with a physician’s note documenting a condition that makes participation unsafe must be excused. A student on a school-sponsored team that practices at least four days a week may also be excused, but only during that team’s season.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated in the policy above?
choices: Lena’s mother submitted a written request, and Lena plays on the school’s volleyball team, which is in season and practices five days a week. So Lena must be excused.
Omar has a physician’s note documenting that his asthma makes participation unsafe, and he has submitted a written request himself. So Omar must be excused.
Theo’s guardian submitted a written request, and Theo has a physician’s note documenting an unsafe heart condition. Although his soccer team is out of season, Theo must be excused.
Priya’s father submitted a written request, and Priya swims for a private club team that is in season and practices six days a week. So Priya may be excused.
Mira’s mother submitted a written request, but Mira has no physician’s note, and her school’s tennis team practices only three days a week. So Mira may not be excused.
questions.explanation: A request from a parent or guardian is required; that request plus a qualifying physician’s note guarantees an exemption; a school-sponsored team only permits one, and only in season. Theo has the request and the note, so he must be excused; his team’s season is beside the point, which makes (C) right. Each trap misses one detail: (A) turns “may” into “must,” (B) has Omar’s own request rather than a parent’s, (D) relies on a team that isn’t school-sponsored, and (E) treats the listed grounds as the only ones.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Excused → written request from a parent or guardian. That request AND unsafe-condition note → must be excused. That request AND school-sponsored team 4+ days AND in season → may be excused.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment the policy actually supports, including its verdict word (must / may / may not).

breakdown.analysis: Sort the rules by type, and read every word of each. Rule 1 is necessary: no request from a parent or guardian → no exemption. Rule 2 is sufficient: request + note → MUST be excused. Rule 3 gives permission, not a guarantee, and only for a school-sponsored team that practices four or more days a week, in season. Notice what the policy doesn’t say: it never says a note or a team are the ONLY grounds. So it can rule a student out only through Rule 1 or the team rule’s limits, and it can require an exemption only through Rule 2. Each wrong answer misses exactly one detail, so check every condition: who made the request, what kind of team, and must versus may. The right answer (C) hides behind a distraction: the out-of-season team looks like a problem, but Theo qualifies through his note.

choices.note: Tempting. Lena is in season and her team practices enough. But the team rule only says she MAY be excused; it doesn’t require it. ‘Must’ overshoots.

Tempting. Omar has the note, and a written request exists. But the policy requires a request from a parent or guardian, and Omar wrote his own. Without a qualifying request, Rule 2 never kicks in, so the policy doesn’t require excusing him.
CORRECT. Theo has a request and a physician’s note documenting an unsafe condition, so Rule 2 says he must be excused. His team being out of season doesn’t matter; he isn’t relying on the team rule.

questions.stimulus: Literary historian: Late in her career, the novelist Edda Raske published three novels under the name “J. Halloran”; that she wrote them was not publicly revealed until after her death. Critics of the day praised the Halloran novels far more warmly than the novels Raske published under her own name in those years, although scholars now agree that the two sets of novels are of comparable quality. So critics’ bias against Raske, not weakness in her writing, explains the cool reception of her late work.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the literary historian’s argument depends?
choices: Raske’s authorship of the Halloran novels was unknown to every one of the critics who reviewed those novels during her lifetime.
The Halloran novels were neither better nor worse written than the novels that Raske published under her own name in those same years.
Critics of Raske’s day did not dislike Raske for reasons that had nothing to do with the novels she wrote.
The critics who reviewed the Halloran novels were the same critics who reviewed the novels Raske published under her own name.
Some of the warm praise for the Halloran novels came from critics who did not take those novels to be Raske’s work.
questions.explanation: The historian treats the warm reception of the Halloran books as a blind test: the same quality of writing got praise when it wasn’t known to be Raske’s. That works only if at least some of the praise was given without taking the books to be hers, which is (E). (A) is the too-strong version: the argument doesn’t need every critic to have been in the dark, and ‘not publicly revealed’ doesn’t even settle that.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Critics’ bias against Raske, not weak writing, explains the cool reception of her late own-name novels.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: She published three novels as “J. Halloran” (authorship revealed only after her death); critics praised them far more than her own-name novels; scholars now judge the two sets comparable in quality.

breakdown.analysis: The quality gap is already closed: the stimulus tells you scholars judge the two sets comparable. So don’t hunt for a quality answer. What’s left? The argument is a blind taste test. Same quality, warmer praise when the name was hidden, so the name was the problem. But ‘not publicly revealed’ isn’t ‘not known.’ If everyone who praised the Halloran books took them to be Raske’s, the test wasn’t blind, and the praise was praise for a known Raske. Then the coolness toward her own-name books can’t be bias against her. We need at least some praise given blind. Use the negation test on every choice.

choices.note: Tempting. It’s the right idea, and it echoes ‘not publicly revealed.’ But it’s too strong. Negate it: one or two critics knew. The argument survives as long as some of the praise came from critics who didn’t take the books to be hers.
choices.negation: At least one critic who reviewed the Halloran novels during Raske’s lifetime knew that she had written them.

choices.note: Not required. The stimulus already says the two sets are comparable, and ‘neither better nor worse’ demands exact equality. Negate it: one set was a bit better or worse. ‘Comparable’ still holds, and the argument stands.
choices.negation: The Halloran novels were either somewhat better or somewhat worse written than Raske’s own-name novels of those years.

choices.note: Reads like a defender, but negate it: critics did dislike Raske for reasons unrelated to her novels. That fits ‘bias against her’ perfectly. Its negation helps the argument, so it can’t be required.
choices.negation: Some critics of Raske’s day disliked her for reasons that had nothing to do with her novels.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument doesn’t need the two groups of critics to be identical. Negate it: some critics reviewed one set but not the other. The overall pattern of praise can still reflect bias.
choices.negation: Not every critic who reviewed the Halloran novels also reviewed Raske’s own-name novels.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: every bit of the praise came from critics who took the books to be Raske’s. Then critics warmly praised work they believed was hers, and the gap in reception can’t be bias against her. The argument needs at least some praise given blind.
choices.negation: None of the warm praise for the Halloran novels came from critics who did not take those novels to be Raske’s work.
